Dengue Cases Reported in Florida; FMCA and Mosquito Control Professionals to Help Prevent Spread News provided by Florida Mosquito Control Association Aug 31, 2026, 10:15 ET Share this article Share toX Share this article Share toX Tallahassee, Fla., Aug. 31, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- With more than 40 confirmed human cases of locally-acquired dengue fever in the state – including more than 30 in the Tampa Bay area - the Florida Mosquito Control Association (FMCA) is urging Floridians to take precautions and help mosquito control professionals across the state reduce the risk of mosquito borne illnesses. The confirmed cases, which prompted the Florida Department of Health in Hillsborough County to issue a mosquito-borne illness alert, underscore the importance of Florida's year-round mosquito surveillance, prevention and control efforts. The locally acquired cases reported in Florida this year include 30 in Hillsborough County, seven in Miami-Dade County, three in Pinellas County and one in Palm Beach County. Hillsborough, Miami-Dade and Pinellas counties are currently under mosquito-borne illness alerts, while Palm Beach County is under a mosquito-borne illness advisory. In Hillsborough County, 10 mosquito pools have also tested positive for dengue virus. "Dengue is not simply an uncomfortable illness—it can be debilitating and, in severe cases, life-threatening," said Peter Jiang, PhD, director of Hillsborough County Mosquito Management and the president of the Florida Mosquito Control Association, (FMCA). "It is sometimes called 'break-bone fever' because of the intense muscle, joint and bone pain it can cause. For Floridians, it is an important reminder that mosquito control is not just about preventing a nuisance; it is an essential public health service that helps protect our residents and communities from mosquito-borne disease." The number of human cases is expected to increase in the state's weekly report. Florida's summertime climate is perfect for mosquitoes, and an influx of visitors – especially in popular destinations like Tampa - enjoying a summer vacation raises the opportunities for diseases to spread. Florida is home to some of the nation's top mosquito control scientists and professionals. Coordinating with the Florida Department of Health surveillance efforts are focused on limiting the spread. "And while success is never final, every resident and visitor to our state should know that Florida remains safe and accessible," he said. "Scientists and highly trained mosquito control professionals work closely with health officials 24/7 to limit the spread of any diseases." The state Department of Health says that dengue can "present as a flu-like illness with severe muscle aches and joint pain, fever, and sometimes a rash." Symptoms appear within 15 days of being bitten by an infected Aedes aegypti mosquito. The disease is not contagious among humans. For more than 100 years, the FMCA has helped scientists and entomologists battle mosquitoes and educate the public about the multitude of dangerous diseases transmitted via a mosquito bite. Currently, Hillsborough County Mosquito Management continues to work closely with the Florida Department of Health and various county and city departments to provide boots on the ground mosquito safety education in areas of concern. Florida's mosquito control efforts focus on scientific discovery and inquiry, front-line deployment of personnel and technology, and a strong network of professionals sharing best practices and experiences. In addition to treating areas where mosquitoes are heavily concentrated, counties use sentinel animals to test for some mosquito-spread diseases. Aircraft and drones can be deployed to treat inaccessible areas. Every Floridian can help, especially during hot weather which speeds up the lifecycle of a mosquito. The American Mosquito Control Association has a summary of measures , calling them the three Ds of protection. Drain –Following a rain or storm, each household and property becomes a virtual resort for mosquitoes looking for a place to breed. Emptying any water in toys or planters or anywhere is a critical and easy step to slow or eliminate the opportunity for mosquitoes to lay eggs. Mosquitoes only need a teaspoon of water to breed, emptying even small accumulations of water outside can make a difference. Dress – Wearing light-colored, loose-fitting clothes are a deterrent to mosquitoes, long sleeves or pants provide even more protection. Defend – Use insect repellants that are registered by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, especially those with DEET. They pose little to no risk for humans but are powerful shields against mosquitoes. There are 67 mosquito control programs in the state, including 15 independent districts that partner with each other and local departments of health to share important news, resources and scientific studies. They also stand ready to respond to any Floridian's request for local mosquito treatment. For more information about the FMCA please click here. And for teachers and parents, the FMCA has resources to inform children about the science and background of mosquitoes and efforts to control them here. news.content: Schedule Football Basketball Recruiting Big Ten Sports BuckeyesXtra Newsletter HEALTH 'Break-bone' dengue virus numbers climbing, threat closing in on SW Florida's Chad Gillis Fort Myers News-Press & Naples Daily News Updated Aug. 31, 2026, 10:04 a.m. ET Dengue fever, also known as "break-bone" virus, is spreading in Florida, with most cases concentrated in the Tampa and Miami areas. The virus is spread solely by the Aedes aegypti mosquito, which thrives in standing water around human homes. While no locally acquired cases have been reported in Southwest Florida, officials urge residents to take precautions. In some places it's known as the "break-bone" virus due to the extreme pain it can cause. Dengue is on a lot of minds in Florida, and Southwest Florida is smack in the middle of the state's two highest concentration of infected residents ― Tampa and Miami. "Dengue fever is called break-bone fever because of how painful it can be," said Keira Lucas deputy executive director of the Collier Mosquito Control District. "And if you get it a second time, it can be deadly." Although no locally contracted cases of dengue fever have been reported in Southwest Florida, mosquito control districts and the Florida Health Department have been preparing for more instances of the potentially deadly virus. "There are more than 40 confirmed cases of locally acquired dengue fever in Florida, but none of them have been in the Collier area,' said Keira Lucas, "But more than 30 of those have been in the Tampa area." The Tampa area is less than a three-hour car drive from the Fort Myers-Naples area, and Lucas said people who travel to the Tampa area should pay special attention to mosquito activity until conditions improve. "We're starting to see more and more locally acquired cases popping up and several counties are under mosquito alerts for dengue," she said. "We want to be proactive. And if our residents are traveling to the Tamps area, take precautions when it comes to mosquito bites." Dengue fever is found in warm, tropical regions, and its spread solely by the Aedes aegypti mosquito. It was present in Florida in the 1930s but was not a health concern here for about 75 years. "Dengue was endemic to the state of Florida but it was eradicated," Lucas said. "And the mosquito that can spread dengue lives in close association with humans. It lives around people's homes and it likes to bite people." The virus returned to the Sunshine State in 2009 and 2010, when 85 cases (some being locally transmitted) were documented in Key West. Since then, dengue fever has been a concern, particularly in south Florida. "In 2011 and 2012, only isolated cases of local (dengue) transmission were reported in Florida, none were reported in Key West," says a report from National Library of Medicine. "In 2013, a new outbreak occurred, but this time in Martin County about 275 miles north of Key West with 22 reported cases." The mosquito that just loves us, sometimes to death Aedes aegypti is a species that has evolved alongside human beings for thousands of years. They really need two things: human blood and standing water. "Its habitat is artificial containers," Lucas said. "Bird baths, buckets, even something as small as a bottle cap can breed hundreds or thousands of Aedes aegypti mosquitoes." Lucas said any standing water around residential areas is fair game for this species as it has adapted to our behaviors. Humans build and keep containers, and sometimes we leave them outside during the rainy season. "It's a good time to go around the home and dump containers of standing water and can use larvicide," she said. "Dengue is only spread by mosquitoes, so it bites another human and then another human. There are no birds involved, like with West Nile virus." West Nile is one of several mosquito-borne viruses, and the others include: eastern equine encephalitis, St. Louis encephalitis, Zika, chikungunya, and yellow fever. Viscous saltwater mosquitoes still problematic in Collier One of the first signs that summer is coming in Southwest Florida is when hordes of saltmarsh mosquitoes take to the air and fly up to 60 miles in search of a blood meal. They typically become problematic during high tide phases in May and tend to become less active as the summer continues. Saltmarsh mosquito eggs are found in sandy, muck-like conditions found along most of the West coast of Florida, from the Tampa area to Naples to Flamingo in Everglades National Park. The saltwater mosquitoes have millions of acres of habitat, and treating them is difficult and sometimes impossible. "We are still seeing an extended saltmarsh season," Lucas said. "The drought conditions can really favor the saltmarsh mosquitoes because we're relying on rain to stick around and allow predators into those areas." SW Florida is home to more than 50 mosquito species While the freshwater Aedes aegypti doesn't travel further than a few hundred feet in its entire life, the saltmarsh variety can travel long distances to find blood meals, a requirement for laying the next horde. "Saltmarsh can travel 60 miles with wind," Lucas said. "We're constantly battling mosquitoes that come from our swamps and the extensive preserve lands we have." Lucas said the freshwater mosquitoes that live near and on our homes may be triggered soon as the near-term forecast calls for rain in the Naples area. "We're expecting rain in the next couple of days and that means outside containers are going go fill up," Lucas said. "And we may see dengue virus here in Collier County. And the district is ready to respond. We're already being proactive about keeping the population low" Dengue risk is high across the globe Dengue fever is common in the Caribbean, Central America, South America, the Middle East, Africa, Southeast Asia, and Pacific Islands, according to the Center for Disease Control and Prevention, or CDC. The CDC says just under half of people on the planet (about 4 billion people) live in areas where dengue is a risk. analysis.brief_en: A locally-acquired case of dengue fever has been confirmed in Orange County, Florida, according to health officials. This marks the first confirmed case in the county, with more than 40 cases reported statewide. The confirmation comes as part of ongoing public health monitoring, and officials have provided information about the signs, symptoms, and prevention of dengue. No further details on the investigation or specific response measures have been reported. The case highlights the need for vigilance against mosquito-borne diseases in the region, especially as the mosquito season continues. Dengue fever is a viral illness transmitted by mosquitoes, and while the exact details of the case remain under investigation, the confirmation underscores the importance of preventive measures and public awareness.

news.content_title: Dengue Patients on Dual Antiplatelet Therapy or Oral Anticoagulants Face More Frequent Bleeding
news.content: Medscape AI News & Perspective Tools & Reference CME/CE More NEW! Ask complex medical questions and find the latest clinical guidance for drugs & conditions with Medscape AI× EN RegisterLog In AI Mode Medscape Medical NewsMedBrief Medbrief Dengue Patients on Dual Antiplatelet Therapy or Oral Anticoagulants Face More Frequent Bleeding September 01, 2026Int J Infect Dis. 2026-08-29;:109087.doi:10.1016/j.ijid.2026.109087 0 Add to Email Alerts TOPLINE Patients with acute dengue infection who were on dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) or oral anticoagulant therapy (OAC) had higher rates of major bleeding within 7 days of diagnosis than those not receiving antithrombotic therapy (ATT), whereas those on single antiplatelet therapy (SAPT) showed major bleeding rates similar to those not receiving ATT at both 7 and 30 days after diagnosis. METHODOLOGY Researchers conducted a single-center, observational study to evaluate real-world bleeding and cardiovascular outcomes in patients with acute dengue infection receiving pre-existing ATT. The study comprised a retrospective cardiovascular cohort that used data from a hospital database to identify patients who developed dengue infection between 2015 and 2022 and an exploratory platelet-monitoring cohort that tracked platelet count and platelet function during dengue illness. Patients in the retrospective cohort were classified into four groups based on pre-existing ATT at dengue diagnosis: no ATT (n = 1493; mean age, 63.2 years; 50.5% men), SAPT (n = 163; mean age, 71.7 years; 67.5% men), DAPT (n = 22; mean age, 70.1 years; 63.6% men), and OAC (n = 15; mean age, 70.3 years; 73.3% men). The exploratory cohort included patients not receiving antiplatelet therapy (n = 6) and those receiving aspirin (n = 2) who underwent serial platelet count and platelet function assessments during dengue illness to evaluate platelet recovery patterns. Outcomes were major bleeding events and major adverse cardiovascular events assessed within 7 and 30 days after dengue diagnosis. TAKEAWAY Patients receiving pre-existing ATT were significantly older and experienced more frequent severe dengue manifestations, including severe plasma leakage and severe organ involvement, than those not receiving ATT (P < .001). Within 7 days of dengue diagnosis, major bleeding rates were 0.34% in the no ATT group, 0.61% in the SAPT group, 4.55% in the DAPT group, and 6.67% in the OAC group (P = .011); major adverse cardiovascular events occurred in 1 patient in the no ATT group and 3 patients in the DAPT group, with no events in the SAPT or OAC groups. Within 30 days of dengue diagnosis, major bleeding rates were 1.15% in the no ATT group, 1.84% in the SAPT group, 9.09% in the DAPT group, and 13.33% in the OAC group (P = .002); major adverse cardiovascular events occurred in 7 patients in the no ATT group, 2 patients in the SAPT group, and 3 patients in the DAPT group, with no events in the OAC group. In the exploratory cohort, recovery of platelet counts and platelet function was slower among patients receiving aspirin than among those not receiving antiplatelet therapy during dengue illness, with median recovery times of 7.5 vs 4.0 days and 9.5 vs 4.0 days, respectively (P = .04 for both). IN PRACTICE "These findings suggest that patients receiving pre-existing ATT, including those receiving SAPT, appeared to represent a clinically vulnerable group in this cohort," the authors wrote. SOURCE The study was led by Po-Tseng Lee, National Cheng Kung University Hospital, Tainan, Taiwan. It was published online on August 29 in International Journal of Infectious Diseases. LIMITATIONS The single-center observational design and nonrandomized treatment allocation resulted in baseline differences in risk across ATT groups. Major bleeding and cardiovascular events were sparse, particularly in the DAPT and OAC groups, which limited the precision and reliability of the estimated risks. Classification of ATT at dengue diagnosis may have led to exposure misclassification because information on treatment adherence, last dose, treatment interruption, resumption timing, platelet thresholds, and anticoagulant intensity was not systematically available. DISCLOSURES The study was supported by a research grant from the National Health Research Institutes and the Ministry of Science and Technology, Taiwan, Republic of China. The authors declared having no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have influenced the reported work. Ask complex medical questions and find the latest clinical guidance for drugs & conditions with Medscape AI× EN RegisterLog In AI Mode Medscape Medical NewsMedBrief Medbrief Dengue Patients on Dual Antiplatelet Therapy or Oral Anticoagulants Face More Frequent Bleeding September 01, 2026Int J Infect Dis. 2026-08-29;:109087.doi:10.1016/j.ijid.2026.109087 0 Add to Email Alerts TOPLINE Patients with acute dengue infection who were on dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) or oral anticoagulant therapy (OAC) had higher rates of major bleeding within 7 days of diagnosis than those not receiving antithrombotic therapy (ATT), whereas those on single antiplatelet therapy (SAPT) showed major bleeding rates similar to those not receiving ATT at both 7 and 30 days after diagnosis. METHODOLOGY Researchers conducted a single-center, observational study to evaluate real-world bleeding and cardiovascular outcomes in patients with acute dengue infection receiving pre-existing ATT. The study comprised a retrospective cardiovascular cohort that used data from a hospital database to identify patients who developed dengue infection between 2015 and 2022 and an exploratory platelet-monitoring cohort that tracked platelet count and platelet function during dengue illness. Patients in the retrospective cohort were classified into four groups based on pre-existing ATT at dengue diagnosis: no ATT (n = 1493; mean age, 63.2 years; 50.5% men), SAPT (n = 163; mean age, 71.7 years; 67.5% men), DAPT (n = 22; mean age, 70.1 years; 63.6% men), and OAC (n = 15; mean age, 70.3 years; 73.3% men). The exploratory cohort included patients not receiving antiplatelet therapy (n = 6) and those receiving aspirin (n = 2) who underwent serial platelet count and platelet function assessments during dengue illness to evaluate platelet recovery patterns. Outcomes were major bleeding events and major adverse cardiovascular events assessed within 7 and 30 days after dengue diagnosis. TAKEAWAY Patients receiving pre-existing ATT were significantly older and experienced more frequent severe dengue manifestations, including severe plasma leakage and severe organ involvement, than those not receiving ATT (P < .001). Within 7 days of dengue diagnosis, major bleeding rates were 0.34% in the no ATT group, 0.61% in the SAPT group, 4.55% in the DAPT group, and 6.67% in the OAC group (P = .011); major adverse cardiovascular events occurred in 1 patient in the no ATT group and 3 patients in the DAPT group, with no events in the SAPT or OAC groups. Within 30 days of dengue diagnosis, major bleeding rates were 1.15% in the no ATT group, 1.84% in the SAPT group, 9.09% in the DAPT group, and 13.33% in the OAC group (P = .002); major adverse cardiovascular events occurred in 7 patients in the no ATT group, 2 patients in the SAPT group, and 3 patients in the DAPT group, with no events in the OAC group. In the exploratory cohort, recovery of platelet counts and platelet function was slower among patients receiving aspirin than among those not receiving antiplatelet therapy during dengue illness, with median recovery times of 7.5 vs 4.0 days and 9.5 vs 4.0 days, respectively (P = .04 for both). IN PRACTICE "These findings suggest that patients receiving pre-existing ATT, including those receiving SAPT, appeared to represent a clinically vulnerable group in this cohort," the authors wrote. SOURCE The study was led by Po-Tseng Lee, National Cheng Kung University Hospital, Tainan, Taiwan. It was published online on August 29 in International Journal of Infectious Diseases. LIMITATIONS The single-center observational design and nonrandomized treatment allocation resulted in baseline differences in risk across ATT groups. Major bleeding and cardiovascular events were sparse, particularly in the DAPT and OAC groups, which limited the precision and reliability of the estimated risks. Classification of ATT at dengue diagnosis may have led to exposure misclassification because information on treatment adherence, last dose, treatment interruption, resumption timing, platelet thresholds, and anticoagulant intensity was not systematically available. DISCLOSURES The study was supported by a research grant from the National Health Research Institutes and the Ministry of Science and Technology, Taiwan, Republic of China. The authors declared having no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have influenced the reported work. news.content: News Sports Entertainment Opinion Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals STATE Dengue surges in Florida with 18 new cases reported in one week Cheryl McCloud USA TODAY NETWORK - Florida Updated Aug. 31, 2026, 12:17 p.m. ET Florida has reported 41 locally acquired dengue cases in 2026, with 18 new cases in a single week; Hillsborough County accounts for 30. Eight Florida counties are under mosquito-borne illness advisories or alerts, including Hillsborough, Miami-Dade, and Pinellas. FDOH recommends DEET-based repellents and a "drain and cover" strategy to reduce mosquito exposure at home. Cases of dengue continue to increase across Florida, with 18 new locally acquired cases reported in one week by the Florida Department of Health. That brings the statewide total of dengue cases to 41 for the year as of Aug. 22. ➤ Meet the mosquito, the world's deadliest animal The mosquito-borne illness is one of several monitored by the agency. Eight counties are under either a mosquito-borne illness advisory or mosquito-borne illness alert. news.content: Just In Pakistan Opinion World Business Sports Tech Life & Style Health Today's Paper Magazines TNS Instep Money Matters YOU US Wednesday September 02, 2026 Today's Paper Prayer Timing Epaper Home Just In Pakistan Opinion World Business Sports Tech Life & Style Health Magazines Instep Money Matters YOU US TNS Risk factors for dengue transmission in existence Islamabad By Muhammad Qasim September 01, 2026 Relatives sit next to patients suffering from dengue fever at a hospital. — AFP/File Rawalpindi:A total of six individuals have so far tested positive for dengue infection from Rawalpindi district this year though the chances of incidence and spread of the infection is higher in the region because all the risk factors including rains, rising temperature, humidity and infected persons or travellers considered to be the most important for appearance of seasonal dengue fever have become very much in existence. Data collected by ‘The News’ on Monday has revealed that to date, a total of 3,450 individuals were screened for dengue fever of which 3,252 were taken as suspected cases of the disease however, only six were confirmed positive for the infection. Data also reveals that the infection has claimed no life in the district so far this year. It is important to mention that the teams of District Health Authority Rawalpindi have been finding the larvae of ‘aedes aegypti’, the vector that causes dengue fever, in abundance during indoor and outdoor surveillance in the district. The daily report prepared on dengue prevention and control by District Health Authority Rawalpindi on Monday has revealed that to date, larvae of ‘aedes’ mosquitoes have been found from a total of 106993 houses and 17,348 spots in the district. It is alarming that the teams of DHA have found larvae of ‘aedes’ mosquitoes from well over 32,000 houses and 4,300 spots in the district in the last two weeks. According to health experts, the situation regarding dengue transmission is well under control at the time yet the stage is set for a possible outbreak of the infection in the coming days or weeks as six individuals have already been tested positive for dengue fever in the district. It is important that confirmation of patients from a region increases the chances of spread of dengue fever. Studies reveal that the population of dengue fever vector fluctuates with temperature, rainfall and humidity. It is high in the rainy season and during the rainy season, the risk of virus transmission by the vector is greater. Epidemiological findings reveal that dengue infections generally occur during or after rain, as an outcome of rise in vector population. Preventing or reducing dengue virus transmission depends entirely on controlling the mosquito vectors or interruption of human-vector contact. Health experts say that individuals should take preventive measures religiously to avoid an outbreak of the infection. It is important that the effects of temperature, humidity and rainfall along with artificial flooding, the man-made watering of lawns, fields and water spillage, are the genuine factors besides movement of infected patients to cause fast spread of the disease. news.content: CubaHeadlines Dengue Type 4 Detected in Las Tunas: Vulnerable Groups Include Children, Pregnant Women, and the Elderly Wednesday, September 2, 2026 by Matthew Diaz Pregnant woman (Reference image) - Image by © Periódico 26 Health officials in Las Tunas have confirmed the presence of dengue serotype 4 in the region, with children, the elderly, pregnant women, and individuals with underlying health conditions identified as the most vulnerable to severe complications. On Wednesday, the state-run newspaper, PeriÃ3dico 26, reported that Dr. Yumara Acosta GarcÃa, the director of the Provincial Center for Hygiene, Epidemiology, and Microbiology, verified that dengue type 4 is currently prevalent in the area. Dr. Acosta emphasized that this serotype presents "greater clinical complexity" and mentioned that confirmed cases are sent to the Pedro KourÃ Institute of Tropical Medicine (IPK) in Havana for quality control and virus typing. Increased Alert and Preventive Measures Authorities have urged the public to take symptoms seriously. "If you experience joint pain, muscle pain, headaches, or fever, see a doctor to promptly identify cases and prevent further complications in this particular area," advised Acosta. The focus is particularly strong on children, the elderly, those with comorbid conditions, and pregnant women, as well as individuals linked to the Maternal and Child Care Program, all considered high-risk for potential complications. Sanitary Offensive and Inspections The confirmation of serotype 4 has prompted provincial authorities to launch a "sanitary offensive," conducting state inspections in workplaces and educational institutions. Workplaces are deemed "sentinels" due to the large number of people they gather. Inspections target the elimination of potential breeding grounds for the Aedes aegypti mosquito and ensure proper coverage of water storage containers. "Our focus from vector control is to prevent the spread of the vector and, consequently, the transmission of the disease from our workers to the broader community," explained the director. Background of Epidemiological Challenges Las Tunas previously faced significant epidemiological challenges. Last November, the province initiated a fumigation campaign in response to rising cases of fever, dengue, and chikungunya, prioritizing areas like Las Tunas, Puerto Padre, Majibacoa, and Jobabo, which had the highest incidence of suspected cases. This current alert is not isolated within the country. In June, the Ministry of Public Health warned of the risk of a new dengue epidemic, acknowledging that all four virus serotypes were circulating simultaneously in Cuba. Deputy Minister Carilda PeÃ±a noted that the dominance of any serotype could trigger localized outbreaks and, without proper measures, lead to an epidemic. More recently, the situation has also raised alarms in GuantÃ¡namo. In mid-August, officials acknowledged an increase in Aedes aegypti mosquitoes and challenges in detecting febrile cases. Serotypes 2, 3, and 4 were confirmed in that province, with several municipalities facing particularly concerning epidemiological situations. Understanding Dengue Type 4 and Its Impact in Cuba What is dengue serotype 4? Dengue serotype 4 is one of the four variations of the dengue virus, each capable of causing dengue fever. Infection with one serotype provides immunity against that serotype but not the others, making subsequent infections potentially more severe. Why are children and the elderly more at risk? Children and the elderly have weaker immune systems, making them more susceptible to severe complications from dengue infections, including dengue hemorrhagic fever and dengue shock syndrome. How is Cuba managing the dengue outbreak? Cuba is implementing sanitary measures including state inspections to eliminate mosquito breeding grounds, focusing on high-risk areas, and ensuring rapid identification and treatment of suspected cases to control the outbreak. news.content_original: CubaHeadlines Dengue Type 4 Detected in Las Tunas: Vulnerable Groups Include Children, Pregnant Women, and the Elderly Wednesday, September 2, 2026 by Matthew Diaz Pregnant woman (Reference image) - Image by © Periódico 26 Health officials in Las Tunas have confirmed the presence of dengue serotype 4 in the region, with children, the elderly, pregnant women, and individuals with underlying health conditions identified as the most vulnerable to severe complications. On Wednesday, the state-run newspaper, PeriÃ3dico 26, reported that Dr. Yumara Acosta GarcÃa, the director of the Provincial Center for Hygiene, Epidemiology, and Microbiology, verified that dengue type 4 is currently prevalent in the area. Dr. Acosta emphasized that this serotype presents "greater clinical complexity" and mentioned that confirmed cases are sent to the Pedro KourÃ Institute of Tropical Medicine (IPK) in Havana for quality control and virus typing. Increased Alert and Preventive Measures Authorities have urged the public to take symptoms seriously. "If you experience joint pain, muscle pain, headaches, or fever, see a doctor to promptly identify cases and prevent further complications in this particular area," advised Acosta. The focus is particularly strong on children, the elderly, those with comorbid conditions, and pregnant women, as well as individuals linked to the Maternal and Child Care Program, all considered high-risk for potential complications. Sanitary Offensive and Inspections The confirmation of serotype 4 has prompted provincial authorities to launch a "sanitary offensive," conducting state inspections in workplaces and educational institutions. Workplaces are deemed "sentinels" due to the large number of people they gather. Inspections target the elimination of potential breeding grounds for the Aedes aegypti mosquito and ensure proper coverage of water storage containers. "Our focus from vector control is to prevent the spread of the vector and, consequently, the transmission of the disease from our workers to the broader community," explained the director. Background of Epidemiological Challenges Las Tunas previously faced significant epidemiological challenges. Last November, the province initiated a fumigation campaign in response to rising cases of fever, dengue, and chikungunya, prioritizing areas like Las Tunas, Puerto Padre, Majibacoa, and Jobabo, which had the highest incidence of suspected cases. This current alert is not isolated within the country. In June, the Ministry of Public Health warned of the risk of a new dengue epidemic, acknowledging that all four virus serotypes were circulating simultaneously in Cuba. Deputy Minister Carilda PeÃ±a noted that the dominance of any serotype could trigger localized outbreaks and, without proper measures, lead to an epidemic. More recently, the situation has also raised alarms in GuantÃ¡namo. In mid-August, officials acknowledged an increase in Aedes aegypti mosquitoes and challenges in detecting febrile cases. Serotypes 2, 3, and 4 were confirmed in that province, with several municipalities facing particularly concerning epidemiological situations. Understanding Dengue Type 4 and Its Impact in Cuba What is dengue serotype 4? Dengue serotype 4 is one of the four variations of the dengue virus, each capable of causing dengue fever. Infection with one serotype provides immunity against that serotype but not the others, making subsequent infections potentially more severe. Why are children and the elderly more at risk? Children and the elderly have weaker immune systems, making them more susceptible to severe complications from dengue infections, including dengue hemorrhagic fever and dengue shock syndrome. How is Cuba managing the dengue outbreak? Cuba is implementing sanitary measures including state inspections to eliminate mosquito breeding grounds, focusing on high-risk areas, and ensuring rapid identification and treatment of suspected cases to control the outbreak. (WWSB) - CDC data shows reported dengue cases have increased in several Florida counties. Hillsborough County rose from 20 reported cases to 36, according to the latest provisional county-level data. Miami-Dade County increased from 49 cases to 67. Broward County increased from 11 to 12 cases. Lee County moved from the CDC’s previous “1 to 4” reporting category to five cases. Because the earlier total was reported as a range, the exact size of the increase cannot be determined from the data provided. Pinellas County remained in the CDC’s “1 to 4” category. That does not necessarily mean the number of cases is unchanged, since the CDC does not provide an exact total for counties in that range. Dengue Fever reported in Tampa, Hillsborough County Palm Beach County remained at seven reported cases. Sarasota and Manatee counties were not listed in the latest county-level CDC table or in the data reviewed for WWSB’s Aug. 26 report. The CDC said its surveillance data is reported by a patient’s county of residence, not necessarily where the person was exposed to the virus. Dengue is a mosquito-borne disease related to the viruses that cause West Nile and yellow fever, according to the Florida Department of Health. The department says it can be painful and debilitating, though it is rarely fatal. Florida health officials say cases are reported each year among people who traveled to places where dengue is present. Those imported cases commonly involve travel to the Caribbean, Central and South America, and Asia. Cyclosporiasis cases rise in Manatee, Sarasota counties Florida’s proximity to areas with dengue, including Puerto Rico, and frequent international travel by residents make it possible for dengue to be reintroduced, the Florida Department of Health said. Sarasota County Mosquito Management also warns that someone who is infected while traveling can return home and be bitten by a local mosquito, which could then pass the disease to another person. Sarasota County Mosquito Management said it regularly monitors mosquito populations for potential disease. The county uses specialized traps to collect mosquitoes, then tests collected mosquitoes for viruses in an on-site molecular laboratory. The county said mosquito season typically peaks from May through October, when warmer temperatures and rain create conditions favorable for mosquitoes. If mosquitoes test positive for a virus, the county said it can increase trapping, investigate possible breeding sites and take other response steps. If a human case is reported, Sarasota County said those efforts continue while the Florida Department of Health gathers information about recent travel that could help determine where the infection was acquired. Sarasota County distinguishes between a mosquito-borne illness advisory and an alert. An advisory means the public should take precautions to reduce mosquito bites because of factors that can indicate local disease activity, such as positive sentinel animals or a small number of presumptive or positive human cases, the county said. An alert indicates heightened disease activity, a significant increase in mosquitoes capable of carrying disease or an increase in locally transmitted human cases, according to the county. CDC data shows a total of 1,575 reported human dengue cases so far in 2026. CDC said its data is provisional and subject to change. Delays in reporting mean state, territorial and local health departments may have more current totals. The data is provisional and subject to change. The CDC also warns that recently reported case numbers may be incomplete because of delays in reporting and data processing. Copyright 2026 WWSB. All rights reserved. (WWSB) - CDC data shows reported dengue cases have increased in several Florida counties. Hillsborough County rose from 20 reported cases to 36, according to the latest provisional county-level data. Miami-Dade County increased from 49 cases to 67. Broward County increased from 11 to 12 cases. Lee County moved from the CDC’s previous “1 to 4” reporting category to five cases. Because the earlier total was reported as a range, the exact size of the increase cannot be determined from the data provided. Pinellas County remained in the CDC’s “1 to 4” category. That does not necessarily mean the number of cases is unchanged, since the CDC does not provide an exact total for counties in that range. Dengue Fever reported in Tampa, Hillsborough County Palm Beach County remained at seven reported cases. Sarasota and Manatee counties were not listed in the latest county-level CDC table or in the data reviewed for WWSB’s Aug. 26 report. The CDC said its surveillance data is reported by a patient’s county of residence, not necessarily where the person was exposed to the virus. Dengue is a mosquito-borne disease related to the viruses that cause West Nile and yellow fever, according to the Florida Department of Health. The department says it can be painful and debilitating, though it is rarely fatal. Florida health officials say cases are reported each year among people who traveled to places where dengue is present. Those imported cases commonly involve travel to the Caribbean, Central and South America, and Asia. Cyclosporiasis cases rise in Manatee, Sarasota counties Florida’s proximity to areas with dengue, including Puerto Rico, and frequent international travel by residents make it possible for dengue to be reintroduced, the Florida Department of Health said. Sarasota County Mosquito Management also warns that someone who is infected while traveling can return home and be bitten by a local mosquito, which could then pass the disease to another person. Sarasota County Mosquito Management said it regularly monitors mosquito populations for potential disease. The county uses specialized traps to collect mosquitoes, then tests collected mosquitoes for viruses in an on-site molecular laboratory. The county said mosquito season typically peaks from May through October, when warmer temperatures and rain create conditions favorable for mosquitoes. If mosquitoes test positive for a virus, the county said it can increase trapping, investigate possible breeding sites and take other response steps. If a human case is reported, Sarasota County said those efforts continue while the Florida Department of Health gathers information about recent travel that could help determine where the infection was acquired. Sarasota County distinguishes between a mosquito-borne illness advisory and an alert. An advisory means the public should take precautions to reduce mosquito bites because of factors that can indicate local disease activity, such as positive sentinel animals or a small number of presumptive or positive human cases, the county said. An alert indicates heightened disease activity, a significant increase in mosquitoes capable of carrying disease or an increase in locally transmitted human cases, according to the county. CDC data shows a total of 1,575 reported human dengue cases so far in 2026. CDC said its data is provisional and subject to change. Delays in reporting mean state, territorial and local health departments may have more current totals. The data is provisional and subject to change. The CDC also warns that recently reported case numbers may be incomplete because of delays in reporting and data processing. Copyright 2026 WWSB. All rights reserved. ORANGE COUNTY, Fla. - Florida health officials have confirmed a locally acquired case of dengue fever in Orange County. The state health department said Wednesday that it's working with Orange County Mosquito Control to expand surveillance and prevention efforts in the affected areas. Dengue cases in Florida By the numbers: More than 40 locally-acquired cases of dengue fever have been confirmed in Florida so far in 2026, along with more than 100 cases of travel-associated cases of dengue, according to the Florida Department of Health. 41: Number of dengue cases acquired in Florida in 2026, through Aug. 22. - Hillsborough: 30 - Miami-Dade: 7 - Palm Beach: 1 - Pinellas: 3 On Sept. 2, the Florida Department of Health reported one confirmed case of dengue in Orange County, which was not yet listed in the Florida Department of Health's weekly report. 109: Number of travel-associated dengue cases reported. - Bay: 1 - Brevard: 2 - Broward: 12 - Duval: 1 - Hillsborough: 6 - Lake: 1 - Lee: 5 - Manatee: 1 - Miami-Dade: 60 - Monroe: 1 - Orange: 2 - Osceola: 1 - Palm Beach: 6 - Pinellas: 1 - Polk: 2 - Sarasota: 1 - Seminole: 1 - St. Johns: 1 - St. Lucie: 3 - Walton: 1 For those cases connected to international travel, the exposure was connected to the following countries: Brazil, Colombia, Cuba, Dominican Republic, El Salvador, Guatemala, Guyana, India, Indonesia, Mexico, Nicaragua, Peru, and Puerto Rico. What is dengue? Dengue is a virus spread through bites from two species of mosquitoes, Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus, according to Florida health officials. Both are found in Florida. When someone is infected, it can lead to dengue fever, a sometimes painful, debilitating disease. While rare, if symptoms are left untreated, it can be deadly. Dengue fever symptoms Symptoms typically appear 3-14 days after being bitten by an infected mosquito, and usually last 4-7 days. Symptoms are similar to those of influenza and other viruses: Sudden fever Severe headache Eye pain Muscle and joint pain Bleeding Vomiting and diarrhea Can it be deadly? Dengue hemorrhagic fever, a more severe form of dengue, is rare, but can be deadly if not recognized and/or treated with supportive care, according to the Florida Department of Health's website. Treatment There is no treatment for dengue fever or dengue hemorrhagic fever. However, people should manage symptoms and complications. Tips for avoiding mosquito bites There are a number of mosquito-borne illnesses found in Florida, including West Nile, Eastern equine encephalitis, St. Louis encephalitis, as well as travel-related illnesses, like chikungunya fever, dengue fever, malaria, yellow fever, and Rift Valley fever. Health officials are urging residents to take steps to prevent mosquito bites: Use insect repellent on exposed skin or clothing Remove standing water to stop mosquitoes from breeding Keep doors, exterior windows closed Orange County Mosquito Control focused on mosquito spraying What they're saying: Orange County Mosquito Control said Wednesday that it would focus its spraying on the type of mosquito known to carry dengue. "This virus is spread only by mosquitoes," said Steve Harrison, Manager of Orange County Mosquito Control, in a statement. "A person can contract dengue only after being bitten by a mosquito carrying the virus. The mosquito becomes infected by biting a person who has the virus." Orange County Mosquito Control regularly sprays for mosquitos around the county, and said all chemicals are approved by the U.S. EPA and are considered to be safe for humans and animals. The Source: This story was written with information from the Florida Department of Health's Orange County office, the Florida Department of Health website on dengue fever, the Florida Arbovirus Surveillance weekly report (ending Aug. 22), and a statement from Orange County Mosquito Control issued on Sept. 2, the same day that the locally-acquired case in Orange County was confirmed. news.content: newsinfo / Headlines Headlines Surge in patients feared Nearly half of Tacloban barangays log dengue cases By: Joey A. Gabieta - Correspondent / @joeygabietaINQ Philippine Daily Inquirer / 04:35 AM September 01, 2026 MOSQUITO CONTROL A resident checks a tire that could collect stagnant water and serve as a breeding site for dengue-carrying mosquitoes. —Tacloban City Information Office photo TACLOBAN CITY, LEYTE, Philippines — Dengue cases in the city have risen to 323 as of Aug. 26, with nearly half of the city’s 138 barangays reporting confirmed cases, prompting health authorities to intensify mosquito-control measures and urge communities to eliminate breeding sites. The City Health Office (CHO) warned that the number of cases could continue to increase in the coming months as more frequent rains create conditions favorable for the breeding of Aedes mosquitoes, which transmit the dengue virus. Dr. Jaime Opinion, a city health official, said barangay officials and residents play a crucial role in preventing further transmission of the disease. Article continues after this advertisement READ: Dengue outbreak declared in Bohol as cases surge FEATURED STORIES NEWSINFO LIST: Class suspensions on Wednesday (Sept. 2) NEWSINFO Ex-DPWH chief Manuel Bonoan says Marcos asked him to resign NEWSINFO Public urged to take precautions amid Metro Manila haze “Our barangay officials and residents are really the main players on this. We at the City Health Office and the Tacloban City Hospital can only help in terms of interventions,” Opinion said in an interview. Opinion said communities should conduct regular cleanup activities in their neighborhoods and homes, particularly in areas where mosquitoes can breed. The Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus mosquitoes that transmit dengue commonly lay their eggs in containers and other places where stagnant water collects, including discarded tires, cans, bottles, buckets, and uncovered water-storage containers. READ: Dengue cases in Cordillera down 3%, but 8 deaths recorded Article continues after this advertisement Densely populated Opinion also noted that many of the barangays reporting dengue cases are densely populated, which could facilitate the spread of the disease. Dr. Gloria Fabrigas, chief of the Tacloban City Hospital, said the facility had treated 180 dengue patients from the start of the year through the previous week. Article continues after this advertisement Of the total, only six patients came from outside Tacloban, she said. Fabregas said 34 percent of the dengue patients treated at the hospital were between 6 and 20 years old, with males accounting for most of the cases in this age group. /cb Your subscription could not be saved. analysis.brief_en: A surge in dengue cases has been reported in Tacloban City, Leyte, Philippines, as of August 26, 2026. Nearly half of the city’s 138 barangays have logged confirmed cases, with the total reaching 323. The Tacloban City Hospital treated 180 dengue patients from the start of the year through the previous week, with only six cases originating outside the city. Health officials have intensified mosquito-control efforts and urged residents to eliminate breeding sites, particularly in densely populated areas. The City Health Office warned that frequent rains could create favorable conditions for Aedes mosquitoes, which transmit the dengue virus, potentially leading to more cases in the coming months. The situation is being actively managed, with community involvement emphasized to prevent further spread.

The confirmed cases, which prompted the Florida Department of Health in Hillsborough County to issue a mosquito-borne illness alert, underscore the importance of Florida's year-round mosquito surveillance, prevention and control efforts. The locally acquired cases reported in Florida this year include 30 in Hillsborough County, seven in Miami-Dade County, three in Pinellas County and one in Palm Beach County. Hillsborough, Miami-Dade and Pinellas counties are currently under mosquito-borne illness alerts, while Palm Beach County is under a mosquito-borne illness advisory. In Hillsborough County, 10 mosquito pools have also tested positive for dengue virus. "Dengue is not simply an uncomfortable illness—it can be debilitating and, in severe cases, life-threatening," said Peter Jiang, PhD, director of Hillsborough County Mosquito Management and the president of the Florida Mosquito Control Association, (FMCA). "It is sometimes called 'break-bone fever' because of the intense muscle, joint and bone pain it can cause. For Floridians, it is an important reminder that mosquito control is not just about preventing a nuisance; it is an essential public health service that helps protect our residents and communities from mosquito-borne disease." The number of human cases is expected to increase in the state's weekly report. Florida's summertime climate is perfect for mosquitoes, and an influx of visitors – especially in popular destinations like Tampa - enjoying a summer vacation raises the opportunities for diseases to spread. Florida is home to some of the nation's top mosquito control scientists and professionals. Coordinating with the Florida Department of Health surveillance efforts are focused on limiting the spread. "And while success is never final, every resident and visitor to our state should know that Florida remains safe and accessible," he said. "Scientists and highly trained mosquito control professionals work closely with health officials 24/7 to limit the spread of any diseases." The state Department of Health says that dengue can "present as a flu-like illness with severe muscle aches and joint pain, fever, and sometimes a rash." Symptoms appear within 15 days of being bitten by an infected Aedes aegypti mosquito. The disease is not contagious among humans. For more than 100 years, the FMCA has helped scientists and entomologists battle mosquitoes and educate the public about the multitude of dangerous diseases transmitted via a mosquito bite. Currently, Hillsborough County Mosquito Management continues to work closely with the Florida Department of Health and various county and city departments to provide boots on the ground mosquito safety education in areas of concern. Florida's mosquito control efforts focus on scientific discovery and inquiry, front-line deployment of personnel and technology, and a strong network of professionals sharing best practices and experiences. In addition to treating areas where mosquitoes are heavily concentrated, counties use sentinel animals to test for some mosquito-spread diseases. Aircraft and drones can be deployed to treat inaccessible areas. Every Floridian can help, especially during hot weather which speeds up the lifecycle of a mosquito. The American Mosquito Control Association has a summary of measures , calling them the three Ds of protection. Drain –Following a rain or storm, each household and property becomes a virtual resort for mosquitoes looking for a place to breed. Emptying any water in toys or planters or anywhere is a critical and easy step to slow or eliminate the opportunity for mosquitoes to lay eggs. Mosquitoes only need a teaspoon of water to breed, emptying even small accumulations of water outside can make a difference. Dress – Wearing light-colored, loose-fitting clothes are a deterrent to mosquitoes, long sleeves or pants provide even more protection. Defend – Use insect repellants that are registered by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, especially those with DEET. They pose little to no risk for humans but are powerful shields against mosquitoes. There are 67 mosquito control programs in the state, including 15 independent districts that partner with each other and local departments of health to share important news, resources and scientific studies. They also stand ready to respond to any Floridian's request for local mosquito treatment. For more information about the FMCA please click here. And for teachers and parents, the FMCA has resources to inform children about the science and background of mosquitoes and efforts to control them here. news.content_zh: 2026 年 8 月 31 日,佛罗里达州报告了 40 多例本地获得的登革热病例,其中希尔斯伯勒县 30 例、迈阿密戴德县 7 例、皮尼拉斯县 3 例、棕榈滩县 1 例。佛罗里达州蚊虫控制协会 (FMCA) 和蚊虫控制专业人员正在努力防止蚊媒疾病的传播。佛罗里达州希尔斯伯勒县卫生部发布了蚊媒疾病警报,强调了全年蚊虫 监测 和控制的重要性。登革热在人类中不会传染,但会引起严重的症状,包括肌肉和关节疼痛、发烧和皮疹。该疾病由埃及伊蚊传播,叮咬后 15 天内出现症状。FMCA 正在与卫生官员和地方部门合作,提供蚊子安全教育并治疗繁殖区。该州有 67 个蚊虫控制项目,包括 15 个独立区,这些项目共同努力共享资源并响应当地的 治疗 请求。暴发 强调需要提高公众意识并采取积极措施来减少蚊子繁殖的机会,例如排出积水和使用驱虫剂。

More Than 40 Locally Acquired Dengue Cases Reported in Florida; FMCA and Mosquito Control Professionals to Help Prevent Spread PR Newswire Mon, August 31, 2026 at 9:15 AM CDT 4 min read Tallahassee, Fla., Aug. 31, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- With more than 40 confirmed human cases of locally-acquired dengue fever in the state – including more than 30 in the Tampa Bay area - the Florida Mosquito Control Association (FMCA) is urging Floridians to take precautions and help mosquito control professionals across the state reduce the risk of mosquito borne illnesses. Florida Mosquito Control Association The confirmed cases, which prompted the Florida Department of Health in Hillsborough County to issue a mosquito-borne illness alert, underscore the importance of Florida's year-round mosquito surveillance, prevention and control efforts. The locally acquired cases reported in Florida this year include 30 in Hillsborough County, seven in Miami-Dade County, three in Pinellas County and one in Palm Beach County. Hillsborough, Miami-Dade and Pinellas counties are currently under mosquito-borne illness alerts, while Palm Beach County is under a mosquito-borne illness advisory. In Hillsborough County, 10 mosquito pools have also tested positive for dengue virus. "Dengue is not simply an uncomfortable illness—it can be debilitating and, in severe cases, life-threatening," said Peter Jiang, PhD, director of Hillsborough County Mosquito Management and the president of the Florida Mosquito Control Association, (FMCA). "It is sometimes called 'break-bone fever' because of the intense muscle, joint and bone pain it can cause. For Floridians, it is an important reminder that mosquito control is not just about preventing a nuisance; it is an essential public health service that helps protect our residents and communities from mosquito-borne disease." The number of human cases is expected to increase in the state's weekly report. Florida's summertime climate is perfect for mosquitoes, and an influx of visitors – especially in popular destinations like Tampa - enjoying a summer vacation raises the opportunities for diseases to spread. Florida is home to some of the nation's top mosquito control scientists and professionals. Coordinating with the Florida Department of Health surveillance efforts are focused on limiting the spread. "And while success is never final, every resident and visitor to our state should know that Florida remains safe and accessible," he said. "Scientists and highly trained mosquito control professionals work closely with health officials 24/7 to limit the spread of any diseases." The state Department of Health says that dengue can "present as a flu-like illness with severe muscle aches and joint pain, fever, and sometimes a rash." Story Continues Symptoms appear within 15 days of being bitten by an infected Aedes aegypti mosquito. The disease is not contagious among humans. For more than 100 years, the FMCA has helped scientists and entomologists battle mosquitoes and educate the public about the multitude of dangerous diseases transmitted via a mosquito bite. Currently, Hillsborough County Mosquito Management continues to work closely with the Florida Department of Health and various county and city departments to provide boots on the ground mosquito safety education in areas of concern. Florida's mosquito control efforts focus on scientific discovery and inquiry, front-line deployment of personnel and technology, and a strong network of professionals sharing best practices and experiences. In addition to treating areas where mosquitoes are heavily concentrated, counties use sentinel animals to test for some mosquito-spread diseases. Aircraft and drones can be deployed to treat inaccessible areas. Every Floridian can help, especially during hot weather which speeds up the lifecycle of a mosquito. The American Mosquito Control Association has a summary of measures , calling them the three Ds of protection. Drain –Following a rain or storm, each household and property becomes a virtual resort for mosquitoes looking for a place to breed. Emptying any water in toys or planters or anywhere is a critical and easy step to slow or eliminate the opportunity for mosquitoes to lay eggs. Mosquitoes only need a teaspoon of water to breed, emptying even small accumulations of water outside can make a difference. Dress – Wearing light-colored, loose-fitting clothes are a deterrent to mosquitoes, long sleeves or pants provide even more protection. Defend – Use insect repellants that are registered by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, especially those with DEET. They pose little to no risk for humans but are powerful shields against mosquitoes. There are 67 mosquito control programs in the state, including 15 independent districts that partner with each other and local departments of health to share important news, resources and scientific studies. They also stand ready to respond to any Floridian's request for local mosquito treatment. For more information about the FMCA please click here. And for teachers and parents, the FMCA has resources to inform children about the science and background of mosquitoes and efforts to control them here. More Than 40 Locally Acquired Dengue Cases Reported in Florida; FMCA and Mosquito Control Professionals to Help Prevent Spread PR Newswire Mon, August 31, 2026 at 9:15 AM CDT 4 min read Tallahassee, Fla., Aug. 31, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- With more than 40 confirmed human cases of locally-acquired dengue fever in the state – including more than 30 in the Tampa Bay area - the Florida Mosquito Control Association (FMCA) is urging Floridians to take precautions and help mosquito control professionals across the state reduce the risk of mosquito borne illnesses. Florida Mosquito Control Association The confirmed cases, which prompted the Florida Department of Health in Hillsborough County to issue a mosquito-borne illness alert, underscore the importance of Florida's year-round mosquito surveillance, prevention and control efforts. The locally acquired cases reported in Florida this year include 30 in Hillsborough County, seven in Miami-Dade County, three in Pinellas County and one in Palm Beach County. Hillsborough, Miami-Dade and Pinellas counties are currently under mosquito-borne illness alerts, while Palm Beach County is under a mosquito-borne illness advisory. In Hillsborough County, 10 mosquito pools have also tested positive for dengue virus. "Dengue is not simply an uncomfortable illness—it can be debilitating and, in severe cases, life-threatening," said Peter Jiang, PhD, director of Hillsborough County Mosquito Management and the president of the Florida Mosquito Control Association, (FMCA). "It is sometimes called 'break-bone fever' because of the intense muscle, joint and bone pain it can cause. For Floridians, it is an important reminder that mosquito control is not just about preventing a nuisance; it is an essential public health service that helps protect our residents and communities from mosquito-borne disease." The number of human cases is expected to increase in the state's weekly report. Florida's summertime climate is perfect for mosquitoes, and an influx of visitors – especially in popular destinations like Tampa - enjoying a summer vacation raises the opportunities for diseases to spread. Florida is home to some of the nation's top mosquito control scientists and professionals. Coordinating with the Florida Department of Health surveillance efforts are focused on limiting the spread. "And while success is never final, every resident and visitor to our state should know that Florida remains safe and accessible," he said. "Scientists and highly trained mosquito control professionals work closely with health officials 24/7 to limit the spread of any diseases." The state Department of Health says that dengue can "present as a flu-like illness with severe muscle aches and joint pain, fever, and sometimes a rash." Story Continues Symptoms appear within 15 days of being bitten by an infected Aedes aegypti mosquito. The disease is not contagious among humans. For more than 100 years, the FMCA has helped scientists and entomologists battle mosquitoes and educate the public about the multitude of dangerous diseases transmitted via a mosquito bite. Currently, Hillsborough County Mosquito Management continues to work closely with the Florida Department of Health and various county and city departments to provide boots on the ground mosquito safety education in areas of concern. Florida's mosquito control efforts focus on scientific discovery and inquiry, front-line deployment of personnel and technology, and a strong network of professionals sharing best practices and experiences. In addition to treating areas where mosquitoes are heavily concentrated, counties use sentinel animals to test for some mosquito-spread diseases. Aircraft and drones can be deployed to treat inaccessible areas. Every Floridian can help, especially during hot weather which speeds up the lifecycle of a mosquito. The American Mosquito Control Association has a summary of measures , calling them the three Ds of protection. Drain –Following a rain or storm, each household and property becomes a virtual resort for mosquitoes looking for a place to breed. Emptying any water in toys or planters or anywhere is a critical and easy step to slow or eliminate the opportunity for mosquitoes to lay eggs. Mosquitoes only need a teaspoon of water to breed, emptying even small accumulations of water outside can make a difference. Dress – Wearing light-colored, loose-fitting clothes are a deterrent to mosquitoes, long sleeves or pants provide even more protection. Defend – Use insect repellants that are registered by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, especially those with DEET. They pose little to no risk for humans but are powerful shields against mosquitoes. There are 67 mosquito control programs in the state, including 15 independent districts that partner with each other and local departments of health to share important news, resources and scientific studies. They also stand ready to respond to any Floridian's request for local mosquito treatment. For more information about the FMCA please click here. And for teachers and parents, the FMCA has resources to inform children about the science and background of mosquitoes and efforts to control them here. news.content: by PERPETUA ETYANG Friday August 7, 2026 Image generated with AI The United States has issued a travel health alert for Kenya following a rise in dengue fever cases, urging travellers to take extra precautions against mosquito bites. In a health alert issued by the US Embassy in Nairobi, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) listed Kenya among countries reporting a higher number of dengue cases in its updated Travel Health Notice. The advisory identifies Kenya's coastal region, as well as Wajir and Garissa counties, as areas where travellers should exercise caution. "Dengue is a mosquito-borne virus common in tropical and subtropical climates that can lead to fever, aches and pains, nausea, and rashes," the embassy said. The embassy urged travellers to consult the CDC's travel health advisories before travelling to affected areas and to take measures to avoid mosquito bites. Recommended precautions include using an Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)-registered insect repellent, wearing long-sleeved shirts and long trousers when outdoors, and sleeping in air-conditioned rooms or rooms fitted with window screens. The alert comes as health authorities continue to monitor dengue infections in several parts of the country, with the disease primarily transmitted through the bite of infected Aedes mosquitoes. The US Embassy advised travellers seeking more information to consult the CDC's travel health guidance or contact the agency directly before visiting affected areas. Dengue is a viral infection that affects millions of people worldwide and is transmitted through the bite of infected mosquitoes. Once diagnosed, it is important to follow medical advice closely, monitor symptoms, and prioritise rest. Adequate hydration plays a crucial role in preventing complications, while nutritious meals help support the body's recovery process. Patients should remain alert to warning signs that may indicate worsening illness and seek immediate medical assistance when necessary. In some cases, hospitalisation may be recommended to ensure close monitoring and appropriate treatment during the recovery period. In May, Garissa county embarked on a massive fumigation exercise aimed at containing the spread of dengue fever following a recent outbreak that has seen several residents hospitalised at the Garissa County Referral Hospital. The two-week exercise, which officially kicked off on Thursday, will involve public health officials fumigating drainage areas, public institutions, schools, markets and other public spaces across Garissa township in an effort to eliminate mosquitoes responsible for spreading the disease. Health officials said samples taken from patients admitted at the Garissa County Referral Hospital confirmed infections of dengue fever, a viral disease transmitted by the Aedes mosquito, which commonly breeds in stagnant water. Speaking to the press after overseeing the launch of the fumigation exercise, Hassan Abdullahi, who was representing the Medical Officer of Health said laboratory tests conducted at the National Public Health Laboratory confirmed the outbreak after 28 out of 40 samples collected from both public and private health facilities tested positive for dengue fever

news.content_original: by PERPETUA ETYANG Friday August 7, 2026 Image generated with AI The United States has issued a travel health alert for Kenya following a rise in dengue fever cases, urging travellers to take extra precautions against mosquito bites. In a health alert issued by the US Embassy in Nairobi, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) listed Kenya among countries reporting a higher number of dengue cases in its updated Travel Health Notice. The advisory identifies Kenya's coastal region, as well as Wajir and Garissa counties, as areas where travellers should exercise caution. "Dengue is a mosquito-borne virus common in tropical and subtropical climates that can lead to fever, aches and pains, nausea, and rashes," the embassy said. The embassy urged travellers to consult the CDC's travel health advisories before travelling to affected areas and to take measures to avoid mosquito bites. Recommended precautions include using an Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)-registered insect repellent, wearing long-sleeved shirts and long trousers when outdoors, and sleeping in air-conditioned rooms or rooms fitted with window screens. The alert comes as health authorities continue to monitor dengue infections in several parts of the country, with the disease primarily transmitted through the bite of infected Aedes mosquitoes. The US Embassy advised travellers seeking more information to consult the CDC's travel health guidance or contact the agency directly before visiting affected areas. Dengue is a viral infection that affects millions of people worldwide and is transmitted through the bite of infected mosquitoes. Once diagnosed, it is important to follow medical advice closely, monitor symptoms, and prioritise rest. Adequate hydration plays a crucial role in preventing complications, while nutritious meals help support the body's recovery process. Patients should remain alert to warning signs that may indicate worsening illness and seek immediate medical assistance when necessary. In some cases, hospitalisation may be recommended to ensure close monitoring and appropriate treatment during the recovery period. In May, Garissa county embarked on a massive fumigation exercise aimed at containing the spread of dengue fever following a recent outbreak that has seen several residents hospitalised at the Garissa County Referral Hospital. The two-week exercise, which officially kicked off on Thursday, will involve public health officials fumigating drainage areas, public institutions, schools, markets and other public spaces across Garissa township in an effort to eliminate mosquitoes responsible for spreading the disease. Health officials said samples taken from patients admitted at the Garissa County Referral Hospital confirmed infections of dengue fever, a viral disease transmitted by the Aedes mosquito, which commonly breeds in stagnant water. Speaking to the press after overseeing the launch of the fumigation exercise, Hassan Abdullahi, who was representing the Medical Officer of Health said laboratory tests conducted at the National Public Health Laboratory confirmed the outbreak after 28 out of 40 samples collected from both public and private health facilities tested positive for dengue fever

news.content: Malaysia's #1 Content Aggregator HomeContact UsAbout UsCareersCreator Back Home/ Local/ Dengue surge in Johor hits nearly 10,000 cases, 13 deaths Dengue surge in Johor hits nearly 10,000 cases, 13 deaths LocalHealth & Fitness 2 Sep 2026 • 1:28 PM MYT Scoop.my News You Can Use, Investigative Reports, Sports, Videos, and Analysis KUALA LUMPUR — Johor has recorded a drastic surge in dengue cases, rising 131.3% for the current period compared to the same period last year. In numbers, the state charted 9,954 dengue cases as of epid week 34 this year compared to 4,304 cases for the same period last year, Bernama reported state health and environment committee chairman Ling Tian Soon saying. Ling said of the total, 4,520 cases or 45.4% were reported from outbreak localities while 5,434 cases or 54.6% were from non-outbreak localities. By location, Ling said Johor Baru recorded the highest number of cases in epid week 34 with 495 cases or 74.6% of the total cases, followed by Kulai (120 cases), Batu Pahat (19), Segamat (nine), Kota Tinggi (seven), Muar and Pontian with four cases each. Johor has also recorded a total of 13 deaths due to dengue up to epic week 33 this year, compared to eight deaths for the same period in 2025, an increase of 62.5%. Last month, Ling said Johor Baru and Kulai were also the main dengue hotspots, accounting for 91% of cases in the state because of their dense populations. He also said the surge in cases was due to the dominant dengue strain — DENV-3 — that is now in circulation. Ling told The Star that this strain causes more severe infections and symptoms. The current hot and dry weather conditions, with intermittent rainfall, is also conducive for the breeding of Aedes mosquitoes which require only a small about of stagnant water. Johor last month approved an allocation of RM116,000 to the Health Department to support fogging operations and also increased the number of community cleaning activities or ‘gotong-royong’. - Sept 2, 2026 The post Dengue surge in Johor hits nearly 10,000 cases, 13 deaths appeared first on Scoop. protection against Dengue and Zika more/close From the Pancera Lab, Vaccine and Infectious Diseases Division August 31, 2026 • By T Vasanthakumar Dengue and Zika are closely related viruses that threaten millions of people worldwide each year. As climate change expands the reach of the mosquitoes that carry these viruses, the development of effective vaccines is becoming increasingly urgent. The close relationship between the two viruses might seem like an advantage for vaccine design. Vaccines work by teaching the immune system to produce neutralizing antibodies, molecules that recognize and bind to a virus and block it from infecting cells. In theory, antibodies that recognize features shared by closely related viruses could provide protection against several of them at once. But with Dengue and Zika, that similarity comes with a catch. Dengue virus exists as four distinct serotypes and infection with one serotype doesn’t necessarily provide lasting protection against the others. Even more concerning, antibodies produced during one infection can sometimes recognize another serotype without effectively neutralizing it. Instead of blocking infection, these antibodies can actually help the virus enter cells and make a subsequent infection more severe. Add the closely related Zika virus to the mix, and the challenge becomes even greater. A successful vaccine must generate broadly neutralizing antibodies, capable of recognizing and blocking multiple related viruses without enhancing infection. Fred Hutch researchers previously discovered one such antibody, F25.S02, isolated from a patient who had experienced multiple exposures to both Dengue and Zika. Understanding exactly how F25.S02 recognizes and blocks all four dengue serotypes as well as Zika could provide valuable clues to design an effective vaccine. Researchers in the Vaccine and Infectious Disease Division at Fred Hutch have now uncovered the structural basis for F25.S02’s remarkable breadth. Led by Nicholas Hurlburt, a staff scientist in the Pancera Lab, the team visualized precisely how F25.S02 binds to viral proteins using cryogenic electron microscopy and X-ray crystallography, two techniques that allow scientists to reveal the structures of biological molecules and their interactions with atomic-level detail. By determining exactly how this antibody interacts with both viruses, researchers have uncovered clues that could help guide the design of next-generation vaccines. The broadly neutralizing antibody F25.S02 (yellow) binds to envelope proteins on the surface of Zika virus (blue). Structural studies revealed that the antibody bridges neighboring envelope proteins, locking them together and preventing the rearrangements needed for viral entry. The inset shows this interaction in atomic detail. Image created by Thamiya Vasanthakumar “By observing the structure of the most broadly neutralizing antibody to all four [Dengue] serotypes and Zika, you can understand its mode of action at the molecular level” explained Hurlburt. The structures revealed that F25.S02 targets a vulnerable seam between proteins found at the surface of the virus. Dengue and Zika viruses are coated in envelope proteins that help them enter human cells. These proteins must dramatically rearrange their structures to bring the viral and host cellular membranes together so they can fuse. This fusion step allows the virus to release its genetic material into the host cell. F25.S02 interferes with this process by binding precisely where two neighboring envelope proteins meet. By bridging this interface, the antibody acts like a molecular lock, holding the proteins together and preventing the rearrangement required for the virus to infect the cell. Importantly, the features recognized by F25.S02 are highly conserved, meaning they remain similar across all four dengue serotypes and Zika virus. While other parts of these viruses vary, this shared vulnerability gives F25.S02 a common target and helps explain its unusually broad protection. For Hurlburt, identifying that weak spot raises the obvious next question: can we make a vaccine that elicits broadly neutralizing antibodies that target this interface? The structural maps determined in this study could provide a roadmap for doing just that. By revealing exactly which features F25.S02 recognizes and how they are arranged in three dimensions, the structures could guide researchers in designing vaccines that direct the immune system toward this shared viral vulnerability and teach it to produce protective broadly neutralizing antibodies. The spotlighted research was supported by the J. B. Pendleton Charitable Trust, Fred Hutch Vaccine and Infectious Disease Division Initiative grant, the Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center Electron Microscopy Shared Resource, the Howard Hughes Medical Institute, and the National Institutes of Health. Hurlburt NK, Lubow J, Goo L, and Pancera M. 2026. Structural basis for antibody cross-neutralization of Dengue and Zika viruses. Communications Biology. DOI: 10.1038/s42003-026-09805-6. Thamiya Vasanthakumar Science Spotlight writer Thamiya Vasanthakumar is a postdoctoral research fellow in the Campbell Lab at Fred Hutch. As a structural biologist, she uses cryogenic electron microscopy (cryoEM) to visualize the molecular structures of receptors found on the surface of immune cells.
