As climate change expands the reach of the mosquitoes that carry these viruses, the development of effective vaccines is becoming increasingly urgent. The close relationship between the two viruses might seem like an advantage for vaccine design. Vaccines work by teaching the immune system to produce neutralizing antibodies, molecules that recognize and bind to a virus and block it from infecting cells. In theory, antibodies that recognize features shared by closely related viruses could provide protection against several of them at once. But with Dengue and Zika, that similarity comes with a catch. Dengue virus exists as four distinct serotypes and infection with one serotype doesn’t necessarily provide lasting protection against the others. Even more concerning, antibodies produced during one infection can sometimes recognize another serotype without effectively neutralizing it. Instead of blocking infection, these antibodies can actually help the virus enter cells and make a subsequent infection more severe. Add the closely related Zika virus to the mix, and the challenge becomes even greater. A successful vaccine must generate broadly neutralizing antibodies, capable of recognizing and blocking multiple related viruses without enhancing infection. Fred Hutch researchers previously discovered one such antibody, F25.S02, isolated from a patient who had experienced multiple exposures to both Dengue and Zika. Understanding exactly how F25.S02 recognizes and blocks all four dengue serotypes as well as Zika could provide valuable clues to design an effective vaccine. Researchers in the Vaccine and Infectious Disease Division at Fred Hutch have now uncovered the structural basis for F25.S02’s remarkable breadth. Led by Nicholas Hurlburt, a staff scientist in the Pancera Lab, the team visualized precisely how F25.S02 binds to viral proteins using cryogenic electron microscopy and X-ray crystallography, two techniques that allow scientists to reveal the structures of biological molecules and their interactions with atomic-level detail. By determining exactly how this antibody interacts with both viruses, researchers have uncovered clues that could help guide the design of next-generation vaccines. The broadly neutralizing antibody F25.S02 (yellow) binds to envelope proteins on the surface of Zika virus (blue). Structural studies revealed that the antibody bridges neighboring envelope proteins, locking them together and preventing the rearrangements needed for viral entry. The inset shows this interaction in atomic detail. Image created by Thamiya Vasanthakumar “By observing the structure of the most broadly neutralizing antibody to all four [Dengue] serotypes and Zika, you can understand its mode of action at the molecular level” explained Hurlburt. The structures revealed that F25.S02 targets a vulnerable seam between proteins found at the surface of the virus. Dengue and Zika viruses are coated in envelope proteins that help them enter human cells. These proteins must dramatically rearrange their structures to bring the viral and host cellular membranes together so they can fuse. This fusion step allows the virus to release its genetic material into the host cell. F25.S02 interferes with this process by binding precisely where two neighboring envelope proteins meet. By bridging this interface, the antibody acts like a molecular lock, holding the proteins together and preventing the rearrangement required for the virus to infect the cell. Importantly, the features recognized by F25.S02 are highly conserved, meaning they remain similar across all four dengue serotypes and Zika virus. While other parts of these viruses vary, this shared vulnerability gives F25.S02 a common target and helps explain its unusually broad protection. For Hurlburt, identifying that weak spot raises the obvious next question: can we make a vaccine that elicits broadly neutralizing antibodies that target this interface? The structural maps determined in this study could provide a roadmap for doing just that. By revealing exactly which features F25.S02 recognizes and how they are arranged in three dimensions, the structures could guide researchers in designing vaccines that direct the immune system toward this shared viral vulnerability and teach it to produce protective broadly neutralizing antibodies. The spotlighted research was supported by the J. B. Pendleton Charitable Trust, Fred Hutch Vaccine and Infectious Disease Division Initiative grant, the Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center Electron Microscopy Shared Resource, the Howard Hughes Medical Institute, and the National Institutes of Health. Hurlburt NK, Lubow J, Goo L, and Pancera M. 2026. Structural basis for antibody cross-neutralization of Dengue and Zika viruses. Communications Biology. DOI: 10.1038/s42003-026-09805-6. Thamiya Vasanthakumar Science Spotlight writer Thamiya Vasanthakumar is a postdoctoral research fellow in the Campbell Lab at Fred Hutch. As a structural biologist, she uses cryogenic electron microscopy (cryoEM) to visualize the molecular structures of receptors found on the surface of immune cells. news.content: Ministry intensifies dengue response in Garissa, Wajir as cases hit 1,678 - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS advertisements HOME NEWS Ministry intensifies dengue response in Garissa, Wajir as cases hit 1,678 Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ By Christine Muchira Friday August 28, 2026 Ad Government has intensified dengue response measures in Garissa and Wajir counties. In a statement from Ministry of Health, communities have been urged to eliminate mosquito breeding sites, prevent daytime mosquito bites and seek prompt medical care for symptoms. The health ministry noted that as at 26 August 2026, Garissa County had recorded 1,583 cumulative reported dengue cases, while Wajir County had recorded 95 laboratory-confirmed cases bringing the total to 1,678 cases. advertisements Five suspected deaths have been also been reported in Garissa County; four in Garissa Township and one in Hagadera. In Garissa, Dadaab accounts for the highest number of reported cases at 1,276, followed by Garissa Township with 251 and Fafi with 56 cases. In Wajir, Wajir East accounts for 85 of the 95 confirmed cases, representing 89.5 per cent. The remaining cases have been reported in Eldas, Wajir West, Wajir North, Wajir South, Tarbaj and Khorof Harar. Ad Children and adolescents aged between six months and 15 years account for 46 of the confirmed cases in Wajir, representing 48.4 per cent. Measures being implemented The Ministry of Health, working with county governments and partners, has activated the Public Health Emergency Operations Centre, supported by continued county and sub-county coordination meetings. Health facilities in affected areas have also been placed on high alert, while suspected dengue samples are being referred to the national reference laboratory for confirmation. Further, the Ministry has strengthened case management and Infection Prevention and Control measures in affected health facilities as well as referral of suspected dengue samples to the national reference laboratory for confirmation, alongside priority investigation and classification of severe cases and suspected deaths. Ad Other measures being implemented include risk communication and community engagement focused on eliminating mosquito breeding sites, preventing daytime mosquito bites and encouraging early healthcare seeking. Dengue is transmitted mainly by infected Aedes mosquitoes, which commonly bite during the day and breed in small collections of stagnant water. The Ministry has urged households, institutions and communities empty, scrub and tightly cover water-storage containers at least once each week, dispose of bottles, tins, tyres and other items that can collect water, and clear blocked drains, use mosquito repellent, long clothing and window or door screens, especially during the day, and protect children from mosquito bites. Members of the public have also been advised to seek care promptly for fever, severe headache, pain behind the eyes, muscle or joint pain, nausea, vomiting or rash, get urgent medical attention for severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, bleeding, breathing difficulty, extreme weakness, restlessness or rapid deterioration. Ad These as well as use paracetamol for fever as directed by a health professional and avoid aspirin or ibuprofen because they may increase bleeding risk. Although no new cases have been reported since the latest county updates, the Ministry has reiterated commitment in sustained surveillance before interruption of transmission can be verified. It will continue working with county governments, health facilities, community health teams and partners to maintain clinical readiness, laboratory confirmation, vector control and timely public information. analysis.location_and_population: The outbreak is reported in Garissa and Wajir counties, specifically in Garissa Township, Dadaab, Fafi, Wajir East, Eldas, Wajir West, Wajir North, Wajir South, Tarbaj, and Khorof Harar. Children and adolescents aged between six months and 15 years account for 48.4% of confirmed cases in Wajir.
analysis.event: The Ministry of Health reported a total of 1,678 dengue cases in Garissa and Wajir counties as of 26 August 2026, with 1,583 cumulative reported cases in Garissa and 95 laboratory-confirmed cases in Wajir. Five suspected deaths were also reported in Garissa County.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Garissa County had the highest number of reported cases at 1,276, followed by Garissa Township with 251 and Fafi with 56. In Wajir, Wajir East accounted for 85 of the 95 confirmed cases. The Ministry has emphasized the need for sustained surveillance to verify the interruption of transmission.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The Ministry has activated the Public Health Emergency Operations Centre, supported by county and sub-county coordination meetings. analysis.brief_en: The Ministry of Health in Kenya has intensified its response to a dengue outbreak in Garissa and Wajir counties, where a total of 1,678 cases have been reported as of 26 August 2026. Garissa County accounted for 1,583 cumulative reported cases, while Wajir County had 95 laboratory-confirmed cases. Five suspected deaths were also reported, with four in Garissa Township and one in Hagadera. Garissa's Dadaab area had the highest number of cases at 1,276, followed by Garissa Township (251) and Fafi (56). In Wajir, Wajir East represented 89.5% of the confirmed cases. The Ministry has activated the Public Health Emergency Operations Centre and is coordinating with county governments and partners. Health facilities are on high alert, and suspected samples are being sent to the national reference laboratory for confirmation. The Ministry has also emphasized the importance of sustained surveillance to verify the interruption of transmission. Measures include eliminating mosquito breeding sites, preventing daytime bites, and encouraging early medical care. Advertisement Updated: 7:10 PM EDT Sep 1, 2026 Editorial Standards i Bernie Montás Reporter Lee County Mosquito Control on alert after Florida records 149 dengue cases Updated: 7:10 PM EDT Sep 1, 2026 Editorial Standards i Bernie Montás Reporter LEE COUNTY, Fla. — One of amateur bird photographer Joe Abel's biggest obstacles isn't capturing the perfect shot during his outings — it's battling mosquitoes. “As I'm walking, you know, I get a bird lined up, and I got to smack myself,” Abel said. Advertisement He admitted that he often forgets to use mosquito repellent. “I carry spray in my car. Most of the time, I forget to put it on,” he said. This rainy season, the risk of mosquito-borne diseases like dengue has increased. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) reports 149 cases of dengue in Florida. The disease, transmitted by mosquitoes, can cause fever, nausea, rashes and pain in the muscles, joints or bones. Jenifer McBride, with the Lee County Mosquito Control District, shared how the disease has personally affected someone she knows. “My best friend's father lives in Puerto Rico, and last summer he was actually hospitalized with dengue,” McBride said. Of the 149 cases in Florida, 110 were contracted while the individuals were traveling. The remaining 39 cases were locally transmitted by mosquitoes. Dengue is transmitted by the Aedes aegypti mosquito, or the backyard mosquito, as McBride calls it. This insect lays eggs in places containing standing water, including bird baths and plants like bromeliads. McBride said the first line of defense against dengue is to dump standing water out of places that contain it. She and her team are on high alert as the disease spreads. “We're always concerned, but it certainly brings a new heightened awareness of being extra concerned, of making sure we're protecting our citizens,” she said. Although Lee County has not reported any locally transmitted dengue cases, McBride emphasized the importance of collaboration among mosquito control districts across the state. “We're all aware that we need to pitch in and make sure that we're not getting anything that's endemic, that we're fighting it and making sure it doesn't become something that we see every day,” she said. Tech As the world gets drier, cholera, West Nile, and dengue can thrive, study finds "We think a water-borne disease should thrive only when there's plenty of water." by Leigh CookAugust 30, 2026 share Facebook Twitter Link Copied! Photo Credit: iStock Drought is often framed as a water shortage problem, but scientists say it can also become a disease problem — and in some cases, a serious one. New research suggests that as landscapes dry out, infections such as cholera, West Nile virus, and dengue may be more likely to spread. Here's what to know According to Grist, a paper in Trends in Ecology and Evolution analyzed nearly 100 studies involving humans and other animals and described a pattern researchers call the "drought-disease paradox." Dry conditions can reduce some disease threats as water sources disappear, but those same conditions can also create opportunities for other pathogens to thrive. The review examined illnesses linked to mosquitoes, contaminated water, and shifting aquatic systems. It found that drought can sometimes coincide with lower cases of schistosomiasis and malaria, even as cholera, West Nile virus, and dengue move in the opposite direction. Tara Stewart Merrill, an aquatic disease ecologist at the Cary Institute of Ecosystem Studies and co-author of the paper, said the finding may sound surprising at first. TCD Picks » Quince Spotlight 💡These best-sellers from Quince deliver affordable, sustainable luxury for all This popular cashmere sweater just got an upgrade Starting at $50 Sleep serenely on these luxury sheets at 50% off retail Starting at $99 You'll love the pockets on this European linen dress Starting at $60 This cotton blazer's price is even smarter than its look Starting at $80 "It's so counterintuitive," she said, per Grist. "We think a water-borne disease should thrive only when there's plenty of water, but in some cases they thrive when there's less water." The paper is also notable because infectious disease research has historically paid more attention to heat than to drought, even as increasingly dry conditions affect many parts of the world. More background Warming air can draw additional moisture from the ground, worsening drought in many places. Citing a United Nations report, Grist said the world had become 77% drier in three decades. The researchers also highlighted outbreaks and case trends that have tracked with drought. Somalia's 2017 drought coincided with nearly 80,000 cholera cases. In California, the 2000s drought coincided with thousands of additional cases of valley fever, and the state's 2014 superdrought was associated with its second-highest tally of West Nile virus cases. In Brazil, Grist reported findings that dengue danger can increase in the months following drought. Drought can also shift when and where mosquito-borne, food-borne, and dust-borne illnesses appear. Georgia Titcomb, a wildlife disease ecologist and assistant professor at Colorado State University, added that when water becomes scarcer or more unevenly distributed, animals may change their movements and cluster at the remaining sources, creating new hotspots for transmission, Grist reported. What can be done? Scientists said better tracking will be a major part of the solution. Improved satellite monitoring could help researchers and officials track shifts in water across landscapes and better anticipate where disease risks may rise. The study also suggested that water management decisions matter. Building dams, expanding irrigation, or otherwise changing how water moves can sometimes create conditions that help pathogens, parasites, or the organisms that carry them. Drought planning may need to include disease prevention alongside water conservation. That can mean paying closer attention to changing mosquito activity, water quality concerns, and the health effects of dust after wet periods are followed by dry ones — a pattern researchers call "weather whiplash." Drought does not always reduce infection risk. In some places, it can instead shift that risk. As Samantha Sambado, a biologist and postdoctoral researcher at Stanford University who was not involved in the study, put it, according to Grist, "Water touches almost every aspect of life. How do we manage this resource, knowing the future will be warmer?" Get TCD's free newsletters for easy tips, smart advice, and a chance to earn $5,000 toward home upgrades. Tech As the world gets drier, cholera, West Nile, and dengue can thrive, study finds "We think a water-borne disease should thrive only when there's plenty of water." by Leigh CookAugust 30, 2026 share Facebook Twitter Link Copied! Photo Credit: iStock Drought is often framed as a water shortage problem, but scientists say it can also become a disease problem — and in some cases, a serious one. New research suggests that as landscapes dry out, infections such as cholera, West Nile virus, and dengue may be more likely to spread. Here's what to know According to Grist, a paper in Trends in Ecology and Evolution analyzed nearly 100 studies involving humans and other animals and described a pattern researchers call the "drought-disease paradox." Dry conditions can reduce some disease threats as water sources disappear, but those same conditions can also create opportunities for other pathogens to thrive. The review examined illnesses linked to mosquitoes, contaminated water, and shifting aquatic systems. It found that drought can sometimes coincide with lower cases of schistosomiasis and malaria, even as cholera, West Nile virus, and dengue move in the opposite direction. Tara Stewart Merrill, an aquatic disease ecologist at the Cary Institute of Ecosystem Studies and co-author of the paper, said the finding may sound surprising at first. TCD Picks » Quince Spotlight 💡These best-sellers from Quince deliver affordable, sustainable luxury for all This popular cashmere sweater just got an upgrade Starting at $50 Sleep serenely on these luxury sheets at 50% off retail Starting at $99 You'll love the pockets on this European linen dress Starting at $60 This cotton blazer's price is even smarter than its look Starting at $80 "It's so counterintuitive," she said, per Grist. "We think a water-borne disease should thrive only when there's plenty of water, but in some cases they thrive when there's less water." The paper is also notable because infectious disease research has historically paid more attention to heat than to drought, even as increasingly dry conditions affect many parts of the world. More background Warming air can draw additional moisture from the ground, worsening drought in many places. Citing a United Nations report, Grist said the world had become 77% drier in three decades. The researchers also highlighted outbreaks and case trends that have tracked with drought. Somalia's 2017 drought coincided with nearly 80,000 cholera cases. In California, the 2000s drought coincided with thousands of additional cases of valley fever, and the state's 2014 superdrought was associated with its second-highest tally of West Nile virus cases. In Brazil, Grist reported findings that dengue danger can increase in the months following drought. Drought can also shift when and where mosquito-borne, food-borne, and dust-borne illnesses appear. Georgia Titcomb, a wildlife disease ecologist and assistant professor at Colorado State University, added that when water becomes scarcer or more unevenly distributed, animals may change their movements and cluster at the remaining sources, creating new hotspots for transmission, Grist reported. What can be done? Scientists said better tracking will be a major part of the solution. Improved satellite monitoring could help researchers and officials track shifts in water across landscapes and better anticipate where disease risks may rise. The study also suggested that water management decisions matter. Building dams, expanding irrigation, or otherwise changing how water moves can sometimes create conditions that help pathogens, parasites, or the organisms that carry them. Drought planning may need to include disease prevention alongside water conservation. That can mean paying closer attention to changing mosquito activity, water quality concerns, and the health effects of dust after wet periods are followed by dry ones — a pattern researchers call "weather whiplash." Drought does not always reduce infection risk. In some places, it can instead shift that risk. As Samantha Sambado, a biologist and postdoctoral researcher at Stanford University who was not involved in the study, put it, according to Grist, "Water touches almost every aspect of life. How do we manage this resource, knowing the future will be warmer?" Get TCD's free newsletters for easy tips, smart advice, and a chance to earn $5,000 toward home upgrades. LEARN MORE » Sections বাংলা Thursday, September 3, 2026 Today's Paper Video e-Paper Second Edition Contact Sections Home Frontpage Asia City World OP-ED Editorial Business Global Business Commercial Capital Sports Countrywide Featured Sex & Relationship Student Vision LitScape Life Style Reciprocal Teens & Twenties In Vogue Food & Nutrition Bookshelf Entertainment Back Page × Facebook Twitter Pinterest Home Back Page Discover more Hospital Health Medical Literature & Resources Published: 11:18 PM, 28 August 2026 Dengue gets indomitable with 342 new admissions in a day The number of dengue patients is on the rise recently. According to the DGHS, as many as 88 people have died of dengue so far this year. The photo was taken from Mugda Medical College & Hospital in the capital on Friday. -Mostafizur Rahman, AA Bangladesh has logged 342 new dengue hospitalizations in the past 24 hours till 8am on Friday, taking the tally of admitted patients to 2,268. No deaths have been reported during the period, according to the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) bulletin issued yesterday. The DGHS said 88 people have died of dengue so far this year, including 34 in August alone. Dhaka North City Corporation hospitals admitted 72 patients, while 43 were admitted under Dhaka South. By division, Barishal recorded 63 admissions, Chattogram 93, Mymensingh 48 and Rangpur 23. Meanwhile, 345 patients were discharged in the same 24-hour window. The DGHS said 32,590 people have been hospitalised with the mosquito-borne disease since Jan 1 this year, of whom 30,422 have recovered. The health directorate has tracked dengue cases since 2000. The worst year on record was 2023, when 321,179 people were hospitalised and 1,705 died, the highest annual toll to date. Last year, dengue killed more than 400 people, with around 102,000 cases recorded. Dengue (break-bone fever) is a viral infection that is spread from mosquitoes to people. It is more common in tropical and subtropical than in temperate climates. Most people who get dengue do not have symptoms. For those who do, the most common symptoms are high fever, headache, body aches, nausea and rash. Most get better in 1-2 weeks. Some develop severe dengue and need care in a hospital. In severe cases, dengue can be fatal. You can lower your risk of dengue by avoiding mosquito bites, especially during the day. Dengue is treated through pain management as there is no specific treatment currently. According to the DGHS, as many as 88 people have died of dengue so far this year. The photo was taken from Mugda Medical College & Hospital in the capital on Friday. -Mostafizur Rahman, AA Bangladesh has logged 342 new dengue hospitalizations in the past 24 hours till 8am on Friday, taking the tally of admitted patients to 2,268. No deaths have been reported during the period, according to the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) bulletin issued yesterday. The DGHS said 88 people have died of dengue so far this year, including 34 in August alone. Dhaka North City Corporation hospitals admitted 72 patients, while 43 were admitted under Dhaka South. By division, Barishal recorded 63 admissions, Chattogram 93, Mymensingh 48 and Rangpur 23. Meanwhile, 345 patients were discharged in the same 24-hour window. The DGHS said 32,590 people have been hospitalised with the mosquito-borne disease since Jan 1 this year, of whom 30,422 have recovered. The health directorate has tracked dengue cases since 2000. The worst year on record was 2023, when 321,179 people were hospitalised and 1,705 died, the highest annual toll to date. Last year, dengue killed more than 400 people, with around 102,000 cases recorded. Dengue (break-bone fever) is a viral infection that is spread from mosquitoes to people. It is more common in tropical and subtropical than in temperate climates. Most people who get dengue do not have symptoms. For those who do, the most common symptoms are high fever, headache, body aches, nausea and rash. Most get better in 1-2 weeks. Some develop severe dengue and need care in a hospital. In severe cases, dengue can be fatal. You can lower your risk of dengue by avoiding mosquito bites, especially during the day. Dengue is treated through pain management as there is no specific treatment currently. news.content: SECTIONS journalism with a human touch Login My Profile Signed In as Profile Change Password Sign out Home Magazine Quick Read India World Sports Business Entertainment Reviews Columns Leisure More Hamburger Web Stories Videos Sci/Tech Health Defence Middle East Maritime Tourism Education Jobs & Career Search Subscribe Specials Middle East Defence Health Maritime × Search results for journalism with a human touch × News India World Sports Business Tourism Sci/Tech Entertainment Jobs & Career Education Magazine The Week Health Opinion Specials Health Defence Middle East Maritime Reviews Movies Books Gadgets Games Multimedia Videos Web Stories Quick Read Leisure Society Lifestyle Services About Us Privacy Policy Terms of Use Contact Us SIGN IN SUBSCRIBE Follow Us News Health Dengue-related kidney injury: Symptoms, risks, and warning signs Dengue can lead to acute kidney injury (AKI), a serious complication often overlooked, especially during monsoon seasons Dr Vikram Kalra Published: August 29, 2026 12:33 PM IST 4 minute Read Share × Email Facebook Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Reddit 0 Comments Link Copied Highlights Dengue can cause acute kidney injury (AKI), a serious but often overlooked complication, especially in severe cases The risk is highest in patients with severe dengue, shock, or dehydration, as these conditions reduce blood flow to the kidneys Early detection is crucial; monitor for warning signs like reduced urine output and seek immediate medical help if symptoms worsen Representation Monsoon season sees dengue emerge as one of the leading diseases carried by mosquitoes. The majority of individuals who are affected recover through proper treatment and management of the disease condition. Nonetheless, dengue can be severe in some individuals and affect vital organs such as the kidneys. Dengue-related acute kidney injury (AKI) is a key issue, though it is often overlooked. It can vary from a temporary decline in renal function to severely debilitating renal failure necessitating constant monitoring or, in exceptional cases, dialysis. The risk factor is generally higher in patients suffering from severe cases of dengue, often resulting in complications such as bleeding, shock, and severe dehydration. How can dengue affect the kidneys? Kidney injury in dengue can be due to various factors. Severe dehydration from fever, vomiting, and reduced fluid intake can decrease blood flow to the kidneys. In severe cases of dengue, plasma leakage can decrease effective circulating blood volume and cause hypotension, leading to inadequate blood supply to the kidneys. Inflammation due to dengue infection may also lead to renal damage. Moreover, complications like muscular injury, bleeding, shock, and electrolyte imbalances can put more pressure on the kidneys. Who is at greater risk? It is not true that every person suffering from dengue is going to develop any sort of kidney damage. However, the risk is higher for those who are suffering from serious dengue, shock, or severe bleeding. People with pre-existing impairment, diabetes, hypertension and other chronic conditions can also be monitored very carefully. What are the warning signs? The problem with acute kidney injury is that it can sometimes manifest with very few symptoms. As a result, a patient may not realise that his kidney function is declining until the damage becomes more serious, which makes it more difficult to treat the condition. The symptoms of acute kidney injury include lack of urine production, dark urine, swelling around the eyes, tiredness, feeling sick and vomiting, difficulty in breathing, confusion, and high blood pressure. It is important to point out that many of these symptoms may occur when a patient has dengue. This is why medical evaluation and laboratory examination are crucial when the patient’s condition is worsening. Another important thing to bear in mind is that just because the fever starts to go down, it doesn’t mean that the patient is recovering from his illness. In fact, critical moments in dengue are known to take place when the fever begins to decline. Therefore, patients should continue looking for any warnings even when their temperature becomes normal. How is kidney injury diagnosed? To evaluate the functioning of the kidneys, doctors can analyse urine production and conduct blood tests called serum creatinine and blood urea tests, which help to determine changes in the kidney filtering process, and electrolytes are studied to identify disruptions in sodium and potassium levels. The doctors might check the blood counts as well as the liver function based on the patient’s condition level and other factors. How is it managed? The treatment strategy will depend on the severity of dengue, hydration level, blood pressure, kidney function, and other complications. Fluid balance is important. Fluid administration must be adequate since both deficiency and excess can be detrimental. On one hand, too much fluid in a dehydrated patient may aggravate kidney injury, whereas too much fluid given to a patient suffering from kidney impairment may cause both fluid overload and respiratory distress. Severe cases of kidney injury must receive supportive care in the hospital, and for certain selected cases, dialysis may be necessary. Prevention starts with early recognition: The optimal method to minimise the chances of severe kidney complications is by detecting the warning signs at an early stage. A person who is infected with dengue should keep track of how much water is taken in and how much urine is produced, as well as listen to what the doctor has to say in terms of fluid intake, medications, and tests. Reduced urine output, continuing vomiting and bleeding, extreme fatigue and weakness, breathlessness, swelling, confusion, and increasing abdominal pain should be reasons for a person to seek immediate medical assistance. Starting off as a simple viral fever, dengue can evolve into more complicated forms in some cases. Monitoring urine output and other symptoms can help diagnose kidney disturbances at an early stage. news.content_original: SECTIONS journalism with a human touch Login My Profile Signed In as Profile Change Password Sign out Home Magazine Quick Read India World Sports Business Entertainment Reviews Columns Leisure More Hamburger Web Stories Videos Sci/Tech Health Defence Middle East Maritime Tourism Education Jobs & Career Search Subscribe Specials Middle East Defence Health Maritime × Search results for journalism with a human touch × News India World Sports Business Tourism Sci/Tech Entertainment Jobs & Career Education Magazine The Week Health Opinion Specials Health Defence Middle East Maritime Reviews Movies Books Gadgets Games Multimedia Videos Web Stories Quick Read Leisure Society Lifestyle Services About Us Privacy Policy Terms of Use Contact Us SIGN IN SUBSCRIBE Follow Us News Health Dengue-related kidney injury: Symptoms, risks, and warning signs Dengue can lead to acute kidney injury (AKI), a serious complication often overlooked, especially during monsoon seasons Dr Vikram Kalra Published: August 29, 2026 12:33 PM IST 4 minute Read Share × Email Facebook Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Reddit 0 Comments Link Copied Highlights Dengue can cause acute kidney injury (AKI), a serious but often overlooked complication, especially in severe cases The risk is highest in patients with severe dengue, shock, or dehydration, as these conditions reduce blood flow to the kidneys Early detection is crucial; monitor for warning signs like reduced urine output and seek immediate medical help if symptoms worsen Representation Monsoon season sees dengue emerge as one of the leading diseases carried by mosquitoes. The majority of individuals who are affected recover through proper treatment and management of the disease condition. Nonetheless, dengue can be severe in some individuals and affect vital organs such as the kidneys. Dengue-related acute kidney injury (AKI) is a key issue, though it is often overlooked. It can vary from a temporary decline in renal function to severely debilitating renal failure necessitating constant monitoring or, in exceptional cases, dialysis. The risk factor is generally higher in patients suffering from severe cases of dengue, often resulting in complications such as bleeding, shock, and severe dehydration. How can dengue affect the kidneys? Kidney injury in dengue can be due to various factors. Severe dehydration from fever, vomiting, and reduced fluid intake can decrease blood flow to the kidneys. In severe cases of dengue, plasma leakage can decrease effective circulating blood volume and cause hypotension, leading to inadequate blood supply to the kidneys. Inflammation due to dengue infection may also lead to renal damage. Moreover, complications like muscular injury, bleeding, shock, and electrolyte imbalances can put more pressure on the kidneys. Who is at greater risk? It is not true that every person suffering from dengue is going to develop any sort of kidney damage. However, the risk is higher for those who are suffering from serious dengue, shock, or severe bleeding. People with pre-existing impairment, diabetes, hypertension and other chronic conditions can also be monitored very carefully. What are the warning signs? The problem with acute kidney injury is that it can sometimes manifest with very few symptoms. As a result, a patient may not realise that his kidney function is declining until the damage becomes more serious, which makes it more difficult to treat the condition. The symptoms of acute kidney injury include lack of urine production, dark urine, swelling around the eyes, tiredness, feeling sick and vomiting, difficulty in breathing, confusion, and high blood pressure. It is important to point out that many of these symptoms may occur when a patient has dengue. This is why medical evaluation and laboratory examination are crucial when the patient’s condition is worsening. Another important thing to bear in mind is that just because the fever starts to go down, it doesn’t mean that the patient is recovering from his illness. In fact, critical moments in dengue are known to take place when the fever begins to decline. Therefore, patients should continue looking for any warnings even when their temperature becomes normal. How is kidney injury diagnosed? To evaluate the functioning of the kidneys, doctors can analyse urine production and conduct blood tests called serum creatinine and blood urea tests, which help to determine changes in the kidney filtering process, and electrolytes are studied to identify disruptions in sodium and potassium levels. The doctors might check the blood counts as well as the liver function based on the patient’s condition level and other factors. How is it managed? The treatment strategy will depend on the severity of dengue, hydration level, blood pressure, kidney function, and other complications. Fluid balance is important. Fluid administration must be adequate since both deficiency and excess can be detrimental. On one hand, too much fluid in a dehydrated patient may aggravate kidney injury, whereas too much fluid given to a patient suffering from kidney impairment may cause both fluid overload and respiratory distress. Severe cases of kidney injury must receive supportive care in the hospital, and for certain selected cases, dialysis may be necessary. Prevention starts with early recognition: The optimal method to minimise the chances of severe kidney complications is by detecting the warning signs at an early stage. A person who is infected with dengue should keep track of how much water is taken in and how much urine is produced, as well as listen to what the doctor has to say in terms of fluid intake, medications, and tests. Reduced urine output, continuing vomiting and bleeding, extreme fatigue and weakness, breathlessness, swelling, confusion, and increasing abdominal pain should be reasons for a person to seek immediate medical assistance. Starting off as a simple viral fever, dengue can evolve into more complicated forms in some cases. Monitoring urine output and other symptoms can help diagnose kidney disturbances at an early stage. The author is the principal director, Nephrology and Kidney Transplant at Aakash Healthcare Multi-Speciality Hospital, Dwarka. news.content: As dengue fever spreads across Tampa Bay, health officials encourage safety measures - Dengue fever cases are on the rise in the Tampa Bay area, with Pasco County confirming a recent case and health officials urging preventative measures. Dengue fever cases are increasing in the Tampa Bay area, and local health officials are asking people to take precautions to prevent the spread. Pasco County confirmed a case of dengue earlier this week. Health officials are investigating how and where the disease was transmitted. The Pasco County case comes after Hillsborough, Pasco and Citrus counties also reported locally acquired cases this month. The Pasco County Mosquito Control District says protection against dengue starts with keeping mosquitoes away from yourself and your home. They suggest the following measures to limit the chances of mosquito bites: - Dump and drain standing water around homes and businesses at least once a week. - Use EPA-registered insect repellent containing an active ingredient such as DEET, picaridin or IR3535. - Cover up with long sleeves, long pants, and socks when possible. - Close doors and keep windows properly screened. - Check your property for small containers and any items that can hold water. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, at least 149 confirmed cases of dengue have been reported in Florida this year — by far the most in the U.S. The latest CDC data, updated as of Aug. 26, lists at least 36 cases reported in Hillsborough County and one to four in Pinellas

news.content: Homepage Latest News Cuba News Miami News Blackouts today Informal Exchange Rate Videos Sports International News Opinion CiberCuba Interviews United States Cuisine Florida Spain Culture Motor Readings Tourism History Nature Health Close the sidebar ESENFRIT Sister of baseball player Héctor Mendoza passes away in hospital in Isla de la Juventud: "She arrived dehydrated and there was no IV." Latest News By CiberCuba Editorial Team Monday, August 31, 2026 - 12:30 María Luisa Mendoza, sister of the Pinero pitcher Héctor MendozaPhoto © Facebook/Swing Completo and Cantalo TV María Luisa Mendoza, 27 years old and sister of the Cuban pitcher Héctor Mendoza, passed away on Saturday at the municipal hospital "Héroes del Baire" in Nueva Gerona, Isla de la Juventud, after being admitted with a case of hemorrhagic dengue at a facility that did not have the necessary serum to treat her, according to the specialized media Swing Completo. A source who spoke with that news outlet described the events harshly: "She arrived dehydrated and there was no IV fluid. The family went out to find the necessary medical supplies, and when they returned, she went into cardiac arrest and couldn’t make it." Intravenous hydration is the essential treatment for hemorrhagic dengue, the severe form of the disease, which can lead to bleeding, shock, and multiple organ failure within a few hours. The health and governmental authorities of the special municipality Isla de la Juventud did not issue any official statement regarding the case. The passing of María Luisa Mendoza occurred at the worst moment for the Cuban hospital system in decades. In February, the Minister of Public Health, José Ángel Portal Miranda, acknowledged that the system was "on the verge of collapse", with no short-term solutions in sight. By April, 461 out of 651 essential medications—over 70% of the basic list—were out of stock in state pharmacies, and many hospitals were lacking pain relievers, antibiotics, suturing materials, and even intravenous solutions. The situation described by the source—serious patient, lack of serum, family going to seek it in the informal market, death during the wait—has been repeated in other documented cases in Cuba during 2025 and 2026. The health crisis coincides with a relentless dengue epidemic. Cuba closed 2025 with over 81,900 reported cases of dengue and chikungunya and at least 65 associated deaths, according to the Pan American Health Organization. The Ministry of Public Health warned in June about a possible dengue epidemic. The following month, Villa Clara confirmed the simultaneous circulation of serotypes DENV-2 and DENV-4, a combination capable of worsening the patient's condition within hours. By the end of August, Sancti Spíritus reported a steady increase in cases. Héctor Mendoza is one of the most recognized pitchers from Isla de la Juventud in the last decade. He made his debut in the National Series in 2011 and was selected for the Cuban national team for the 2014 Central American Games, the 2015 Pan American Games, and the Premier12 that same year. He later pitched for the Yomiuri Giants in Japan and in June 2017 signed with the St. Louis Cardinals for the minor leagues in the U.S., an organization that released him in 2019. As of the closing of this note, neither the player nor any other family member had made public statements regarding the death of María Luisa Mendoza. This event is confirmed based on the report from the specialized media Swing Completo.

The situation has been described as the worst moment for the Cuban hospital system in decades, with a severe dengue epidemic ongoing. The risk is highlighted as critical due to the lack of medical resources and the severity of the disease.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Health and governmental authorities in Isla de la Juventud did not issue any official statement regarding the case. The health crisis is ongoing, with no short-term solutions in sight, and the Cuban hospital system is under significant strain. analysis.brief_en: María Luisa Mendoza, the 27-year-old sister of Cuban baseball player Héctor Mendoza, died in the hospital in Isla de la Juventud on August 29, 2026, after being admitted with hemorrhagic dengue. According to the report from specialized media Swing Completo, she arrived dehydrated and the hospital lacked the necessary serum for treatment. The family attempted to find the required medical supplies but failed, leading to her cardiac arrest and death. This incident highlights the severe challenges faced by the Cuban hospital system, which has been under strain since February 2026. By April 2026, over 70% of essential medications were out of stock, and hospitals were lacking critical supplies like intravenous solutions. The health crisis coincides with a dengue epidemic, with Cuba reporting over 81,900 cases and at least 65 deaths by the end of 2025. The authorities in Isla de la Juventud did not issue any official statement on the case, and the situation is described as the worst for the Cuban hospital system in decades. The report also notes that the lack of medical resources and the severity of the disease have been documented in other cases in Cuba during 2025 and 2026.

elements_zh.scale_impact_and_risk: 玛丽亚·路易莎·门多萨 (María Luisa Mendoza) 的死亡是一个个案,但它反映了古巴更广泛的健康危机,截至 2026 年 4 月,古巴 651 种基本药物中有 461 种缺货,医院缺乏静脉注射液等关键物资。目前的情况被描述为古巴医院系统几十年来最糟糕的时刻,重症登革热 疫情仍在持续。由于缺乏医疗资源和疾病的严重性,该风险被强调为严重。

news.content_zh: 2026 年 8 月 29 日,古巴棒球运动员埃克托·门多萨 (Héctor Mendoza) 的 27 岁妹妹玛丽亚·路易莎·门多萨 (María Luisa Mendoza) 因出血性登革热入院,在青年岛的医院去世。据专业媒体Swing Completo报道,她到达时已脱水,医院也缺乏治疗所需的血清。家人试图寻找所需的医疗用品但失败,导致她心脏骤停并死亡。这一事件凸显了古巴医院系统面临的严峻挑战,该系统自2026年2月以来一直处于紧张状态。到2026年4月,超过70%的基本药物缺货,医院缺乏静脉注射液等关键物资。健康危机与登革热疫情同时发生,截至 2025 年底,古巴报告了超过 81,900 例病例,至少 65 人死亡。青年岛当局没有就该病例发表任何官方声明,目前的情况被描述为古巴医院系统几十年来最糟糕的情况。报告还指出,2025 年和 2026 年古巴的其他病例也记录了医疗资源匮乏和疾病严重的情况。

FOX 35 Orlando Gainesville News - FOX 51 Gainesville Atlanta News - FOX 5 Atlanta About Us Meet the FOX 13 team TV Listings Jobs & Internships WTVT History Closed Captioning FCC Public File FCC Applications Contact Us FOX Tampa Bay Live Stream live Interviews & segments Stream on FOX One NFL Live Streaming College Football Live Streaming MLB Live Streaming NASCAR Live Stream IndyCar Live Streaming Men's College Basketball Live Stream Women's College Basketball Live Stream WNBA Live Stream MLS Live Stream Bay Area dengue cases rise to 33 as mosquito spraying ramps up By Joe Espy Health Published September 1, 2026 12:53 PM EDT Published September 1, 2026 12:53 PM EDT Local Dengue fever cases on the rise 0:00 2:25 ▶ PREVIOUS COVERAGE: Local Dengue fever cases on the rise Hillsborough County's Mosquito Management is stepping up its response as the number of Dengue fever cases rise. FOX 13's Aaron Mesmer reports. The Brief Bay Area dengue fever cases jumped to 33 locally acquired infections as health officials issue countywide warnings. Hillsborough County Mosquito Management Services is launching aerial spray runs over South Tampa and Ybor City to stop transmission. Health officials urge residents to empty standing water around homes and follow basic mosquito defense steps. TAMPA, Fla. - Locally acquired dengue fever cases in the Bay Area have climbed to 33, prompting mosquito control agencies in Hillsborough and Pinellas counties to ramp up surveillance, inspections and spraying, according to the Florida Mosquito Control Association (FMCA). The FMCA said Monday that Florida has recorded more than 40 confirmed locally acquired dengue cases this year, including 30 in Hillsborough County and three in Pinellas County. Hillsborough and Pinellas counties are under mosquito-borne illness alerts from the Florida Department of Health. Bay Area dengue fever cases By the numbers: The latest cases represent a significant increase from the numbers reported earlier this summer, which included 10 locally-acquired cases that were reported in the Bay Area last month. PREVIOUS: Dengue fever: 10 locally-acquired cases reported in Tampa Bay Statewide, the locally acquired cases include: 30 in Hillsborough County Seven in Miami-Dade County Three in Pinellas County One in Palm Beach County That brings the statewide total to 41 confirmed locally acquired cases. In Hillsborough County, mosquito surveillance has also detected dengue virus in 10 mosquito pools, according to the FMCA. Locally acquired cases mean the virus was transmitted by mosquitoes in the area rather than being associated with travel. Dengue is mainly spread by infected Aedes aegypti mosquitoes, which are active during the day and can breed in very small amounts of standing water around homes. Hillsborough mosquito spraying Local perspective: Hillsborough County Mosquito Management Services said crews are increasing mosquito treatments by air and ground because mosquito traps in neighborhoods are showing dengue virus activity. The county previously planned aerial applications Monday night in the Seffner and Brandon areas. On Tuesday night, mosquito control crews will conduct additional aerial applications in South Tampa and Ybor City. The Hyde Park treatment is scheduled from 8:30 p.m. Tuesday through 6 a.m. Wednesday in an area bounded by I-275, Bayshore Boulevard and West Watrous Avenue, the Hillsborough River and Hillsborough Bay, and South Manhattan Avenue. The Ybor City treatment is scheduled between 4 and 6 a.m. Wednesday in an area bounded by I-4, the Lee Roy Selmon Expressway, North 39th Street and North Taliaferro Avenue. County officials said alternate spray dates are scheduled for Tuesday and Wednesday if weather or other conditions prevent the treatments. Residents can contact Hillsborough County Mosquito Management Services at 813-635-5400 for more information. Pinellas dengue response Dig deeper: Pinellas County Mosquito Control is also increasing its response as the number of locally acquired dengue cases grows across the Tampa Bay region. Crews are focusing on ground inspections and daytime fogging in Palm Harbor and St. Petersburg, while continuing surveillance and treatments throughout the county. Officials are also conducting door-to-door inspections to identify and eliminate mosquito breeding sites on private property. "Dengue does not stop at county lines," Pinellas County Mosquito Control Director Alissa Berro said. "The mosquitoes that transmit the virus generally stay within a relatively small area, but people travel throughout the Tampa Bay area every day. When someone infected with dengue enters a new area, a local mosquito can bite that person and later spread the virus to others. As cases rise across the region, so does the potential for additional local transmission in Pinellas County." Because the mosquitoes that spread dengue often breed on private property, officials say residents play an important role in reducing the risk of additional transmission. Protecting yourself from dengue What you can do: Health and mosquito control officials are urging residents to follow the 3 Ds: Dress: Wear light-colored, long-sleeved clothing and closed-toed shoes when outdoors. Defend: Use an insect repellent with a CDC-recommended ingredient, including DEET, picaridin, IR3535 or oil of lemon eucalyptus. Dump: Empty or cover standing water around homes, including water in buckets, toys, plant saucers, tires and other containers. Officials say mosquitoes can breed in extremely small amounts of water, making it important to regularly check yards and other outdoor areas. Dengue fever symptoms Why you should care: The FDOH says dengue can cause a flu-like illness with fever, severe muscle aches and joint pain and sometimes a rash. Symptoms can appear within about 15 days after a person is bitten by an infected mosquito. Dengue is not spread through ordinary person-to-person contact. Anyone experiencing symptoms should contact a health care provider and mention any potential exposure to mosquitoes. What they're saying: Peter Jiang, director of Hillsborough County Mosquito Management and president of the FMCA, said dengue can be debilitating and, in severe cases, life-threatening. The disease is sometimes called "break-bone fever" because of the intense muscle, joint and bone pain it can cause, according to Jiang. Mosquito control agencies are continuing to coordinate with the Florida Department of Health on surveillance, education and treatment as the number of cases is expected to increase in the state's upcoming weekly report. For Bay Area residents, officials say one of the most effective ways to help prevent further spread is to eliminate standing water around their homes while taking steps to prevent mosquito bites. The Source: The information in this story was gathered from official updates provided by the Florida Mosquito Control Association, Hillsborough County Mosquito Management Services, Pinellas County Mosquito Control, and the Florida Department of Health. FOX 13's Aaron Mesmer reports. The Brief Bay Area dengue fever cases jumped to 33 locally acquired infections as health officials issue countywide warnings. Hillsborough County Mosquito Management Services is launching aerial spray runs over South Tampa and Ybor City to stop transmission. Health officials urge residents to empty standing water around homes and follow basic mosquito defense steps. TAMPA, Fla. - Locally acquired dengue fever cases in the Bay Area have climbed to 33, prompting mosquito control agencies in Hillsborough and Pinellas counties to ramp up surveillance, inspections and spraying, according to the Florida Mosquito Control Association (FMCA). The FMCA said Monday that Florida has recorded more than 40 confirmed locally acquired dengue cases this year, including 30 in Hillsborough County and three in Pinellas County. Hillsborough and Pinellas counties are under mosquito-borne illness alerts from the Florida Department of Health. Bay Area dengue fever cases By the numbers: The latest cases represent a significant increase from the numbers reported earlier this summer, which included 10 locally-acquired cases that were reported in the Bay Area last month. PREVIOUS: Dengue fever: 10 locally-acquired cases reported in Tampa Bay Statewide, the locally acquired cases include: 30 in Hillsborough County Seven in Miami-Dade County Three in Pinellas County One in Palm Beach County That brings the statewide total to 41 confirmed locally acquired cases. In Hillsborough County, mosquito surveillance has also detected dengue virus in 10 mosquito pools, according to the FMCA. Locally acquired cases mean the virus was transmitted by mosquitoes in the area rather than being associated with travel. Dengue is mainly spread by infected Aedes aegypti mosquitoes, which are active during the day and can breed in very small amounts of standing water around homes. Hillsborough mosquito spraying Local perspective: Hillsborough County Mosquito Management Services said crews are increasing mosquito treatments by air and ground because mosquito traps in neighborhoods are showing dengue virus activity. The county previously planned aerial applications Monday night in the Seffner and Brandon areas. On Tuesday night, mosquito control crews will conduct additional aerial applications in South Tampa and Ybor City. The Hyde Park treatment is scheduled from 8:30 p.m. Tuesday through 6 a.m. Wednesday in an area bounded by I-275, Bayshore Boulevard and West Watrous Avenue, the Hillsborough River and Hillsborough Bay, and South Manhattan Avenue. The Ybor City treatment is scheduled between 4 and 6 a.m. Wednesday in an area bounded by I-4, the Lee Roy Selmon Expressway, North 39th Street and North Taliaferro Avenue. County officials said alternate spray dates are scheduled for Tuesday and Wednesday if weather or other conditions prevent the treatments. Residents can contact Hillsborough County Mosquito Management Services at 813-635-5400 for more information. Pinellas dengue response Dig deeper: Pinellas County Mosquito Control is also increasing its response as the number of locally acquired dengue cases grows across the Tampa Bay region. Crews are focusing on ground inspections and daytime fogging in Palm Harbor and St. Petersburg, while continuing surveillance and treatments throughout the county. Officials are also conducting door-to-door inspections to identify and eliminate mosquito breeding sites on private property. "Dengue does not stop at county lines," Pinellas County Mosquito Control Director Alissa Berro said. "The mosquitoes that transmit the virus generally stay within a relatively small area, but people travel throughout the Tampa Bay area every day. When someone infected with dengue enters a new area, a local mosquito can bite that person and later spread the virus to others. As cases rise across the region, so does the potential for additional local transmission in Pinellas County." Because the mosquitoes that spread dengue often breed on private property, officials say residents play an important role in reducing the risk of additional transmission. Protecting yourself from dengue What you can do: Health and mosquito control officials are urging residents to follow the 3 Ds: Dress: Wear light-colored, long-sleeved clothing and closed-toed shoes when outdoors. Defend: Use an insect repellent with a CDC-recommended ingredient, including DEET, picaridin, IR3535 or oil of lemon eucalyptus. Dump: Empty or cover standing water around homes, including water in buckets, toys, plant saucers, tires and other containers. Officials say mosquitoes can breed in extremely small amounts of water, making it important to regularly check yards and other outdoor areas. Dengue fever symptoms Why you should care: The FDOH says dengue can cause a flu-like illness with fever, severe muscle aches and joint pain and sometimes a rash. Symptoms can appear within about 15 days after a person is bitten by an infected mosquito. Dengue is not spread through ordinary person-to-person contact. Anyone experiencing symptoms should contact a health care provider and mention any potential exposure to mosquitoes. What they're saying: Peter Jiang, director of Hillsborough County Mosquito Management and president of the FMCA, said dengue can be debilitating and, in severe cases, life-threatening. The disease is sometimes called "break-bone fever" because of the intense muscle, joint and bone pain it can cause, according to Jiang. Mosquito control agencies are continuing to coordinate with the Florida Department of Health on surveillance, education and treatment as the number of cases is expected to increase in the state's upcoming weekly report. For Bay Area residents, officials say one of the most effective ways to help prevent further spread is to eliminate standing water around their homes while taking steps to prevent mosquito bites. The Source: The information in this story was gathered from official updates provided by the Florida Mosquito Control Association, Hillsborough County Mosquito Management Services, Pinellas County Mosquito Control, and the Florida Department of Health. supplementary_news.content: Find us on Google 📌 America's birthday 🎂 Start the day smarter ☀️ Get the USA TODAY app U.S. Politics Sports Entertainment Life Money Travel Opinion Crossword ONLY AT USA TODAY: Newsletters For Subscribers Real Estate From the Archives USA TODAY PLAY Crossword Marvel Comics eNewspaper Magazines Investigations Video Podcasts Humankind Advertise Your Business WITNESS (True Crime) Just Curious Best-selling Booklist Top Workplaces Nomination Legals Press Releases Cars Grocery Shopping OUR PORTFOLIO: Real Estate 10BEST USA TODAY Store Shopping Blueprint WITNESS (True Crime) Southern Kitchen Home Internet Services STATE Dengue fever Add Topic Dengue surges in Florida with 18 new cases reported in one week Cheryl McCloud USA TODAY NETWORK - Florida Updated Aug. 31, 2026, 12:17 p.m. ET Hear this story Florida has reported 41 locally acquired dengue cases in 2026, with 18 new cases in a single week; Hillsborough County accounts for 30. Eight Florida counties are under mosquito-borne illness advisories or alerts, including Hillsborough, Miami-Dade, and Pinellas. FDOH recommends DEET-based repellents and a "drain and cover" strategy to reduce mosquito exposure at home. Cases of dengue continue to increase across Florida, with 18 new locally acquired cases reported in one week by the Florida Department of Health. That brings the statewide total of dengue cases to 41 for the year as of Aug. 22. ➤ Meet the mosquito, the world's deadliest animal The mosquito-borne illness is one of several monitored by the agency. Eight counties are under either a mosquito-borne illness advisory or mosquito-borne illness alert. Shop Amazon for mosquito repellents Here's what you should know about mosquito-borne illnesses in Florida, symptoms to watch for and how best to prevent mosquito bites. How many types of mosquito-borne illnesses are there in Florida? FDOH compiles weekly data on the following mosquito-borne viruses in a report called "Florida Arbovirus Surveillance": West Nile virus (WNV) Eastern equine encephalitis virus (EEEV) St. Louis encephalitis virus (SLEV) Dengue virus (DENV) Chikungunya virus (CHIKV) Zika virus (ZIKV) California encephalitis group viruses (CEV) Malaria Mosquito-borne illness alerts, advisories issued for these Florida counties A mosquito-borne illness advisory has been issued for the following counties: Alachua Leon Palm Beach Pasco Walton A mosquito-borne illness alert has been issued for the following counties: Hillsborough Miami-Dade Pinellas "A mosquito-borne illness advisory means the public should take precautions to reduce mosquito bites due to factors indicating local disease such as positive sentinels, very few presumptive or positive human cases, or other justifications," according to Sarasota County. "A mosquito-borne illness alert means that there has been heightened disease activity, a significant increase in vector (disease capable) mosquito populations, or an increase in locally-transmitted human cases. "Residents should continue to take precautions, but exercise additional caution in preventing mosquito bites." Is dengue spreading in Florida? See counties reporting mosquito-borne illnesses According to the Florida Department of Health, as of Aug. 22, there have been 41 cases of locally acquired cases of dengue reported, along with 2 cases of West Nile Virus: Dengue: 41 cases 30 in Hillsborough County 7 in Miami-Dade County 1 in Palm Beach County 3 in Pinellas County West Nile: 2 1 in Alachua County 1 in Walton County Dengue in Florida: What symptoms should you watch for? "Dengue fever can be a painful, debilitating disease but is rarely fatal," the Florida Department of Health said. Symptoms appear three to 14 days after the bite of an infected mosquito and include: sudden onset of fever severe headache eye pain muscle and joint pain (giving the disease the nickname “breakbone fever”) bleeding Gastrointestinal symptoms like vomiting and diarrhea may also be present in some cases. "Dengue fever symptoms usually lasts four to seven days. The disease is often diagnosed incorrectly because the symptoms are similar to influenza and other viruses." Is dengue contagious? Dengue is spread by mosquitoes. Mosquitoes become infected with dengue after biting a person with the virus. Those infected mosquitoes then spread the virus to other people through bites. The Centers for Disease Control said a woman who is infected with the dengue virus during pregnancy could pass the virus to her fetus, causing death to the fetus, low birth weight or premature birth. What are symptoms of West Nile virus? "West Nile virus is a mosquito-borne flavivirus that causes mild to severe illness," the Florida Department of Health said. "Approximately 80% of people who are infected with WNV will not show any symptoms at all." Mild symptoms include: fever headache body aches nausea vomiting Sometimes swollen lymph glands or a skin rash on the chest, stomach and back. Symptoms can last from a few days to several weeks. About one in 150 people infected with West Nile will develop severe illness. Symptoms include: high fever headache neck stiffness stupor disorientation coma tremors convulsions muscle weakness vision loss numbness paralysis "These symptoms may last several weeks, and neurological effects may be permanent. Severe illness can also result in death," FDOH said. "Zika symptoms usually last for several days to a week," FDOH said. "People usually do not get sick enough to go to the hospital. For this reason, many people might not realize they have been infected." What are the best mosquito repellents to use? According to the Florida Department of Health, repellents with the following active ingredients provide the best protection: DEET Picaridin IR3535 Oil of lemon eucalyptus Para-menthane-diol 2-undecanone, a plant-derived ingredient 'Drain and cover' helps keep mosquitoes away The FDOH offered this advice to help keep mosquitoes away from your Florida home: Drain Drain water from garbage cans, old tires, pool covers, or any other containers where water collects. Empty and clean birdbaths and pet water bowls at least once or twice a week. Protect boats and vehicles from rain with tarps that don’t accumulate water. Maintain swimming pools in good condition and ensure they are appropriately chlorinated. Empty plastic swimming pools when not in use. Cover If you must be outside when mosquitoes are active, cover up. Apply mosquito repellent to exposed skin and clothing. Use mosquito netting to protect children younger than 2 months old.
